activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
Lauren had tried on three shirts in twenty minutes, and the bed was now a field of rejected cotton, each shirt an encumbrance she had carried around for years without ever really wearing. The blue one made her look like a substitute teacher. The striped one belonged to a version of herself she no longer believed in. She settled on plain gray and sat down at her laptop to check the bus schedule, which was absurd, because the date wasn't for three hours, but checking something felt better than doing nothing.

Timothe arrived at four, letting himself in the way he had since they were nine, and flopped across the foot of her bed with a groan so lugubrious it could have won an award. "You're going to be late to your own date if you keep rearranging your face," he said, gesturing at the mirror. "You look fine. You look like a person."

"You're a comfort," Lauren said, but she put down the eyeliner.

He was quiet for a moment, which was unlike him, and she watched him in the mirror deciding whether to say something. That was the thing about Timothe: you could see the whole machinery of him working, nothing hidden. "It's Boston," he said finally. "You've seen her at lunch, right? With that guy she's been seeing since the spring. He keeps grabbing her arm. Not, like, playfully. Hard enough that she has to pull it back."

Lauren turned around on the bench. "Grabbing her arm how?"

"Like she's a handle. She laughs after, every time, like it's a bit, but the laugh comes late." He sat up. "I keep almost saying something and then I don't, because what if I'm reading it wrong? What if I make it weird between us? She'd be mortified. She'd say I was being dramatic."

The afternoon light had moved across the carpet while he talked, and Lauren thought about how easy it was to delimit the whole question down to Timothe's cowardice or courage, as if that were the only variable. She pulled the laptop toward her instead of answering right away. She had read something months ago, for a health paper she'd half forgotten, and she typed until she found it again, the numbers sitting on the screen exactly where she'd left them in her memory.

"Okay," she said. "I looked this up for Mr. Murphy's class last semester. In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence." She turned the screen toward him. "One in twelve. Of everybody. That's like two kids in our homeroom."

Timothe read it twice, his lips moving slightly. "So it's not rare," he said. "It's not, like, a thing that happens to other people in other places."

"It's a thing that happens at a rate," Lauren said. "And it doesn't tell you whether it's happening to Boston. That's the part I can't get past. The number makes it real, but it doesn't make it hers." She was aware of her own date waiting at the end of the evening, of the clock, of the strange doubling of the day: she was preparing to be looked at with desire while trying to figure out whether her friend was being hurt. Both things could be true at once. The number said they coexisted all the time, one in twelve, ordinary as bus schedules.

Mr. Murphy was out front with his hedge trimmers when they left to find Boston, and he waved them over to admire his work, and Lauren stood there in her gray shirt making conversation about boxwood while every second stretched. He asked who the young man was that she was meeting later, because word traveled even on their quiet street, and Lauren said, "His name's Ryan," and watched Timothe's face change.

"Ryan," Timothe repeated, once they were past the hedge. "Ryan who's been seeing Boston since the spring?"

Lauren stopped on the sidewalk. The street was very ordinary, sprinklers, a dog, someone's dinner through an open window, and inside that ordinariness she replayed every time she had stood near him at parties, every story Boston had told laughing, every laugh that came late. She had been getting dressed for three hours for a person whose hands she now could not stop picturing, and none of the numbers had anything to do with her until this exact second, except that they had had everything to do with her, one in twelve, all along, and she had read it as homework.

They found Boston on her front steps, phone in her lap, a bruise-colored shadow on her wrist that she turned away when Lauren sat down. Timothe started to speak and then didn't, and Lauren took the phone out of her own pocket and opened the thread with Ryan and typed while both of them watched, and she read it aloud as she wrote it: "Something came up. Not going to make it tonight." Then she set the phone face down on the concrete between the three of them, like a card nobody wanted to pick up, and said to Boston, "Tell me about your arm."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that if F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a).
story:
The community centre had once been a bank, and the tutoring tables still sat in what had been the lobby, under a ceiling rose nobody had the heart to remove. Jacob spread his graph paper across the marble counter where people had once deposited paycheques, and drew rectangles under a curve, twenty of them, then forty, his pencil going blunt.

His exam was in eleven days. He had promised his mother, and the promise had a specific shape: pass the calculus, keep the scholarship, and thereby expiate two years of doing just enough to get by. She hadn't used the word expiate. She had said, "You owe yourself," which amounted to the same thing.

Antonin dropped into the chair beside him with a slushie the colour of a warning label. "You're counting squares."

"I'm summing rectangles. There's a difference."

"There really isn't, visually."

Jacob showed him: the rectangles' tops cut the curve, some area left over, some extra, and if he made them thinner the error shrank but never quite died. He wanted the exact area under the curve from one to four, and he was beginning to suspect the honest answer involved infinity, which felt less like mathematics than a threat.

Damien arrived twenty minutes late, as constitutionally, and put his phone face down with ceremony. "Ms. Ramos said you signed up for the Tuesday slot."

"I signed up for the table."

"Same thing here. This place is a technocracy. Whoever has the worksheet has the power." Damien stole the slushie, drank, and returned it with the straw bent. Jacob ignored this, because Damien was better at calculus than he was and they both knew it, and generosity toward the strong was a kind of self-interest.

Ms. Ramos came by on her rounds with a mug that read WORLD'S ADEQUATE TEACHER. She looked at the rectangles, at the forty little sums marching across his page, and said nothing at all. She tapped the corner of his sheet once and moved on to the girl struggling with limits two tables over. Her silence was vitriolic in its politeness, Jacob thought, or possibly she just trusted him, and he couldn't decide which was worse.

He worked the sums anyway, out of stubbornness, out of a need to see the wall before going around it. 0.3 plus 0.3, times the height at the left edge, again and again, the total creeping toward something like 8.1, then with eighty rectangles 8.25, then 8.3. He could feel where it was going without being able to say the number. That was when Antonin, who had been scrolling through the course notes on his phone with the air of a man reading a court summons, said, "Wait. Look at this thing. It's called the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus."

Damien leaned over. "It says if F is an antiderivative of f, the integral of f from a to b equals F of b minus F of a."

"That's it? Two steps?"

"That's the whole empire," Damien said. "People fought over who found it first."

Jacob found the antiderivative on his own before they could say more: the function was three x squared, so F was x cubed, and he wrote F of four minus F of one, sixty-four minus one, sixty-three, and sat back. Sixty-three. His rectangles had been crawling toward it from below like a congregation toward a shrine, and the theorem simply walked in the front door. All that arithmetic had not been wasted, though; it was how he knew the short answer was true, that the two roads met, and he felt the meeting in his chest before he could have argued it aloud. He still didn't understand why the two roads met, only that they did, and he wrote a small question mark beside his work and did not erase it.

Ms. Ramos drifted past again, glanced at the sixty-three, and at the question mark beside it, and set a fresh sheet of paper next to his elbow. On it, a harder curve, and at the bottom, in her looping hand: because you asked.

Jacob picked up the pencil. Antonin raised the slushie in a small toast to no one.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: A useful way to predict temperature effects is to treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction and as a reactant of an endothermic one.
story:
The gym smelled of hot glue and vinegar, and by ten in the morning Elizabeth had adjusted her poster board three times without admitting to herself that she was stalling. Her project sat at the center of the table: three sealed tubes of nitrogen dioxide gas in a sand bath, a beaker of ice water, a kettle she'd been allowed to borrow from the teachers' lounge on the condition that she indemnify the school against any burns, a promise she'd signed for on a yellow index card.

"It's the good one," Amari said, sliding into the chair beside her. Amari had built a wind turbine two tables over and had already been judged, which made her either a spy or a friend. "Mr. Lin is doing the chemistry rows. He's the one who failed my brother's project for bad labeling."

"My labels are fine."

"Your labels are fine. Your explanation isn't." Amari pointed at the middle section of the board, where Elizabeth had written that cooling the tubes would shift the reaction toward the colorless side, and then, in pencil, crossed it out and written the opposite, and then crossed that out too. "Which is it?"

Elizabeth put her hand flat over the scribbles. "It depends which direction the reaction is exothermic." She heard how it came out, defensive and vague at once, and hated it. At her grandmother's house last weekend she had copied the equation onto a paper towel and stared at it through an entire episode of whatever her grandmother was watching, and the paper towel had ended up in the bin with nothing solved.

"Then find out before he gets here."

The kettle ticked as it cooled. Elizabeth lifted the first tube with tongs, held it in the ice water, and counted under her breath. The brown faded from the bottom of the tube upward, went nearly clear. She set it back in the warm sand and watched the color bleed back in, slow as tea steeping. So cold pushed it toward colorless, and heat pushed it toward brown. She knew what she had seen. What she couldn't do was say why, and Mr. Lin was the kind of judge who asked why until you were standing in the wreckage of your own poster.

Amari leaned in. "You're being pugnacious about a gas."

"I'm thinking."

"You're glaring."

Elizabeth pulled the paper towel memory back up. She had been at the kitchen table, her grandmother offering her a butterscotch, and she had wanted so badly to make the problem behave that she had taken her pencil and written the word heat onto the equation, on the right side, after the products, as if it were another product. Then it had made sense. Cold meant less heat meant less of the products meant the colorless side. It was a trick, a fake, and she had crumpled the paper towel because it felt like cheating, like drawing a moustache on the Mona Lisa to make her like it better.

She found a fresh index card and wrote it again. Heat on the right.

"What's that?" Amari asked.

"Treat heat like a product," Elizabeth said. "If the reaction gives off heat, the heat goes with the products. Take the heat away, and it makes more products to replace it. That's why the tube goes clear in the ice." She tapped the card. "And it would run the other way too. If a reaction takes heat in, then heat acts like a reactant. Add heat, you're adding a reactant, and it pushes forward."

"That's not on your board."

"No."

"So put it on your board."

"It's not real. Heat isn't a chemical. You can't have molecules of heat."

Amari turned the card around to face herself and read it, lips moving slightly. "Does it work?"

Elizabeth looked at the two tubes, the clear one warming back to amber, the dark one. "It works. It predicted everything I just did. I just don't know if it's a rule or a mnemonic."

"It's a science fair. Everything's a mnemonic until someone gives it a prize."

Elizabeth laughed before she could stop it, and there was Mr. Lin, two tables away, holding a clipboard, pausing at Sami's project on water filtration. Sami caught Elizabeth's eye over Mr. Lin's shoulder and mouthed something that was either good luck or a warning.

She uncapped the marker. At the top of the middle section she wrote, in letters large enough to read from the aisle, Le Chatelier's principle, and beneath it, smaller: treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction, and as a reactant of an endothermic one. She left the crossed-out pencil underneath, visible, because hiding it felt like a different kind of cheating. Then she poured the last of the kettle's warm water into the ice beaker, took up the tongs, and set the darkest tube into it.

"Watch," she said, as Mr. Lin turned toward her table.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Mark 2:27, Jesus says that the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath, answering critics of his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath.
story:
The argument started over pancakes, which Victor thought was unfair, because his grandmother made pancakes specifically so that nobody could fight at her table. He had come to her house every Sunday since he was small, first with his mother, now on his own, and this was the first Sunday he would leave early. Practice had been moved to noon because the regional meet was in six days, and his event was the mile, and the coach did not negotiate.

"Sunday is not for running," his grandmother said, setting the syrup down with a small click, the way other people slam doors. "It is for rest. That rule is older than this house."

Victor had prepared for this, though he hadn't known he was preparing until he opened his mouth. His debate class had spent three weeks on a question Ms. Shin had written on the board in her narrow handwriting: whether an ancient religious rule still binds us when the world that made it is gone. She had forbidden them to argue from opinion. Only the text itself, she said, or nothing. Victor had drawn the Sabbath, which he'd thought would be easy, and had spent those three weeks discovering it wasn't.

He reached into his backpack, still at the table, and found the index card he'd written on Thursday night. "Grandma, there's this verse. Mark, chapter two, verse twenty-seven. Jesus says the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath."

She went still over the griddle. "Say that again."

"The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath," Victor said. "He said it because people were criticizing his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath. The disciples were hungry, and they picked grain, and the critics said that was work, that it broke the rule. And that was his answer." He had read the passage eleven times, and each time the sentence seemed to turn differently in his hand, like a stone with more faces than he expected.

His grandmother sat down across from him, which she did not usually do until the dishes were done. "You found that yourself," she said, not as a question. "Nobody gave it to you." She looked out the window at the sugar maple that dominated her small yard, arboreal and patient, dropping its helicopters into the gutters she would pay Carl's older brother to clean next month. "That verse is real. He said it. So you think that means the rule bends whenever a person wants something."

"That's not what I said."

"It's what you're doing with it."

That afternoon, at practice, Victor ran badly. He kept composing sentences in his head, arguing with a woman who wasn't there. Cassidy noticed, matching him on the cooldown jog, and asked what was wrong, and Victor told her the whole thing, the pancakes, the index card, the look on his grandmother's face when she'd sat down.

"You preempted her," Cassidy said. "You came in with your card ready. Nobody likes being handed a verdict before they've been heard."

That evening his grandmother texted him, which she did rarely and formally, as if the phone were a typewriter. I looked it up, the message read. Your verse is there, in Mark, just as you said. I read the whole chapter. The critics were watching him all day, waiting to catch him. That part I had forgotten. Come next Sunday if you must run. We will eat after. He read it four times. He noticed what it did not say, that he had won, that she agreed the rule could bend. It said only that she had gone and looked, alone, at the same words he had looked at alone, and that supper would wait for him now, which was its own kind of answer and its own kind of cost, because waiting had never been her way of conceding anything.

The next morning Ms. Shin asked the class who wanted to argue the negative, the position that the ancient rule still binds. Victor raised his hand before he could talk himself out of it. At the front of the room he laid out the verse, the critics, the grain, the sentence that seemed to cut one way and then, if you sat with it, cut another, because a rule made for man could still be a rule, and a man who kept it wasn't necessarily its slave. Cassidy caught his eye from the second row. "So which is it?" she said, when he finished.

"That's what I keep trying to figure out," Victor said. "My grandmother thinks I know. I'm not sure she's wrong."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Linguist Merrill Swain's output hypothesis holds that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn.
story:
The festival occupied the whole of Riverside Park, and Luca found the debate tent between the churro stand and a stage where a folk troupe was tuning instruments. A hand-lettered sign read, in Portuguese, "Speak for five minutes. Win a book." Luca had studied Portuguese for two years, mostly alone, mostly reading. He had never once argued in it.

Chace had dragged him here. "You said you wanted practice," Chace said, already filling out the entry slip at the folding table. "Here's practice with stakes."

The stakes were a paperback dictionary and a crowd of maybe eleven people on folding chairs. A woman from the language school drew the topic from a jar and read it: should the city ban the festival fireworks over the river, given the smoke that hung in the neighborhood for days afterward. Luca knew the issue. Two summers ago a neighbor, Mr. Gallagher, had stood on his porch at midnight, coughing, waving at the haze drifting down the street while shells burst red over the water. Mr. Gallagher had played cards with Luca's grandfather for thirty years and considered the fireworks an inheritance, noxious smoke included. "My lungs can complain to the historians," he had said that night, ash settling on his railing. "They'll write it down as beautiful."

Luca took the pro-ban side because it was drawn for him. He had five minutes, and the timer was a woman's phone laid face up on the table.

He began the way he always began, in his head, in English, with a structure: claim, evidence, concession. Then he tried to say that the city's own air monitor had registered the smoke at unsafe levels for two nights running, and he stopped. He did not know the word for monitor. He did not know the word for register, or levels, or unsafe. He circled his hand and said, in Portuguese, "the machine that measures the bad air said the air was bad," and a man in the third row nodded, and Luca felt the gap open under him like a stair missing in the dark. Reading, he had understood everything. Speaking, he could not even report a fact.

He got out the word for smoke. He got out the word for river, for children, for the old man on his porch. When he tried to say that no amount of tradition could exculpate the city for what it put into people's lungs, he lost the verb entirely and had to say instead, "tradition does not erase the wrong," which was blunter, and which he found he liked better. Somewhere in the fourth minute he abandoned English altogether and started building sentences out of the Portuguese he actually owned, short and plain, and the argument changed shape. It stopped being about air-quality indices and became about Mr. Gallagher coughing on his porch while calling it beautiful, about the festival's own historiography, the way its pamphlets recorded every queen and every parade route and never once mentioned the smoke. "The history of the festival," Luca said, in Portuguese, "remembers what it wants."

He used his last minute on the concession, because in English he would have and he wanted to find out whether he could. He said that his grandfather had met people he loved at this festival, that a ban would take something real, and that he did not know whether cleaner air was worth the loss, and that he suspected the answer depended on whose lungs you asked. The timer went off while he was still holding the word for "suspected" in his mouth, not quite able to place it.

Afterward Chace bought him a limeade. "You went blank, like, four times."

"I didn't go blank," Luca said. "I found holes. It's different." He told Chace about a linguist he'd read the winter before, Merrill Swain, whose idea had a name. "She called it the output hypothesis," he said. "Trying to speak makes you notice the gaps in what you know. Reading hid mine. Talking pried them open." Chace looked at him over the cup. "So blanking is the lesson."

"Blanking is the map," Luca said. "Every hole I found is a thing I can go learn tonight."

The anti-ban debater, a college student with a beard, won the dictionary. Luca stayed to shake his hand, and they argued for another ten minutes at the edge of the tent, in a lurching half-Portuguese, the student supplying verbs and Luca supplying the neighbor's porch, the ash, the midnight coughing. The folk troupe started up behind them, drums carrying over the river where the fireworks would go that night if the council kept stalling.

Mr. Gallagher was at the churro stand when Luca came out. "I heard you in there," he said. "Sounded like you were against the fireworks."

"I was assigned the side," Luca said.

"Ah," said Mr. Gallagher, and handed him a churro, and pointed his cane at the river. "Then watch tonight and decide for yourself."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs, so the performer plays it twice before the development begins.
story:
The choir room at St. Brigid's smelled of candle wax and old hymnals, and on Thursday afternoons Mr. Lau let Mia use the upright piano in the corner while he sorted sheet music for Sunday. She had brought her theory workbook, a printout of Mozart's K. 545 first movement, and a pencil with a good eraser. The unit test was in nine days, and she still could not hear where the exposition ended and the development began.

Nikola came with her that Thursday because his mother ran the food pantry in the church basement and he had nowhere else to wait. He put his earbuds in and lay across two folding chairs while Mia played the opening eight bars, stopped, and wrote a bracket in the margin. She played them again. She had chosen a recording to follow along with, a pianist named someone whose name she had already forgotten, and she kept losing her place because the audio kept doing something she could not account for.

"Your pianist is broken," Nikola said from the chairs. "He keeps playing the same part twice. I thought you said these people don't make mistakes."

Mia paused the recording and looked at the score. At the end of the first section there were two thick lines with two dots, facing backward, and the matching pair sat near the very beginning. She had copied them onto her printout without thinking, the way she copied everything. She set the pencil down and played the recording from the start, watching the bars go by, and when the pianist reached the double bar he did not continue. He went back.

"It's the repeat signs," she said. "He plays the exposition twice before the development starts. It's not a mistake." Nikola pulled out one earbud and said that seemed like showing off, and Mia said maybe, but it was written into the music, not invented in the studio.

She marked the exposition with a square bracket, then played the second pass all the way through and listened for what changed. Almost nothing, she decided. The dynamics were a little different, a phrase shaped softer the second time, and she wrote that in the margin too, small, in case it mattered. When the music finally moved on, the sound changed character so gradually that she had to rewind twice to find the exact bar. She drew a vertical line and labeled it "development" and did not feel certain about it at all.

The part she kept circling was the recapitulation. Her teacher had described it in class with a diagram on the whiteboard, an arch that returned home, and Mia had copied the diagram and understood nothing. The idea felt like something you could reify by drawing it, a shape that pretended to be the music without containing any of it. She could see the arch. She could not hear it.

That night she sent a message to Maeva, who had finished the same unit the year before and now tutored for money. "How do you find the recapitulation," Mia typed, "when the second theme sounds almost the same as the first time and the whole thing just slides?" Maeva's reply came as a voice note, and Mia played it while lying on her bed with the score on her chest. "Look at bar one," Maeva said. "Memorize the opening. Then when you're lost in the development, wait. The opening comes back, but it's not in the same key anymore. First time it moves away, second time it stays." Mia sat up and found bar one and put her finger on it.

The twist was that Maeva sent a second message, text this time, an hour later: "Also I looked at my old test. I got the recapitulation bar wrong. They marked it two bars after where I put it, because of a little transition chord I counted as still development. So don't trust me fully." Mia read it twice. She had been ready to copy Maeva's answer the way she copied diagrams, and now even the tutor's authority had a hole in it.

On Sunday she arrived early, before the pantry opened, and found Mr. Lau testing the organ pipes for the service. She asked if she could use the piano again and he said the choir room was open. Then he asked what she was working on, and she said Mozart, sonata form, and he said the organ loft had a recording of K. 545 on cassette from decades of choir warmups, if the machine still worked. It did. She put it on and followed her printout, and when the pianist doubled back at the end of the exposition she did not even flinch; she just wrote "2nd time" above the bracket and kept her pencil moving.

Somewhere in the middle of the development she stopped labeling. The music had gone somewhere she could not name, through keys that felt like a different phylum of the same species, related but strange, and she let it carry her for a full minute with the pencil resting on her knee. Then the opening came back, unmistakable, but landing differently, settled, staying where it was. She drew the line and wrote "recapitulation" beside it, and beside that she wrote a question mark, small enough that only she would ever see it, and left it there. Outside, through the diaphanous curtain over the choir room window, she could see Nikola hauling a box of cans toward the pantry door. She waved, and he waved back with the hand that wasn't holding the box.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: The margin of error measures only random sampling error; it does not cover errors from badly worded questions, people refusing to answer, or poorly conducted interviews.
story:
The line outside the church hall moved in small, patient shuffles, and Kaitlyn stood at a folding table near the doors with a clipboard, a stack of surveys, and the feeling that she had finally been given something adult to do. Ms. Gupta, the returning officer, had requisitioned the table for the students that morning, along with two chairs and a roll of tape, and had told them only, "Stay behind the line and don't block the exit." Beyond that they were on their own, which was exactly what Kaitlyn had wanted.

She and Lucas had argued about the survey for a week. It was meant to capture how the new voters in their district felt about the transit referendum, and Lucas had written the question himself: "Do you agree that the transit plan, which most experts say is wasteful, deserves your support?" He'd printed eighty copies before she saw the wording. When she called it loaded, he'd waved her off and pointed at the bottom of the page, where he had copied a statistic from a website: margin of error plus or minus four percent, based on a sample of ninety.

"That's the whole point of the margin," Lucas had said, sliding copies across the cafeteria table. "It tells you how wrong the number can be. Four percent either way. That's science."

Charles-Antoine, who was working the other door, had looked at the question over her shoulder that morning and laughed, not unkindly. "You might as well ask people if they enjoy being mugged," he said, and then taken his half of the stack and gone to the east entrance, where he was now persuading an old man in a tweed cap to hold his pencil-stub while he filled in the box with his own pen, against the form's instructions.

Kaitlyn watched the voters come through. An old woman in a raincoat stopped at the table, read the question upside down, and said, "Which experts?" before walking on without answering. A young father with a toddler on his shoulders said "no comment" twice, once to Kaitlyn and once to the toddler, as if rehearsing a position. By eleven they had thirty-one responses, twenty-four of them agreeing with a question that agreed with itself, and Kaitlyn had begun to feel that the stack in front of her was not measuring anything except the shape of Lucas's sentence.

She thought about her mother, who had spent one summer years ago phoning strangers for a market research firm and had come home each night with stories of slammed receivers. Her mother had quit by August. "Nobody tells you," she'd said at the time, stirring soup, "how many people just won't pick up, and what kind of people those are." Kaitlyn had been nine and hadn't understood what that had to do with soup or with anything. Now, watching voter after voter wave off Charles-Antoine's clipboard at the east door, she thought she was beginning to.

When the line thinned at noon, she pulled Lucas behind the table, out of the traffic of the polling clerks carrying ballot boxes to the count room, and laid the two stacks side by side. "Look at who's answering," she said. "The people who stop are the ones who already have an opinion and want to say it. The ones who refuse, we never hear from. They're just gone from the number."

"That's what the margin is for," Lucas said. "Plus or minus four."

"No," Kaitlyn said. It came out more firmly than she'd planned, and she lowered her voice, aware of Ms. Gupta checking a voter's card two tables away. "The margin of error only measures random sampling error. It doesn't cover a badly worded question, or people refusing to answer, or interviews done badly. None of that's in the four percent."

Lucas looked at his own sentence on the page for a long moment. "So the number's wrong by more than it says it's wrong by."

"Wrong in a direction," Kaitlyn said. "That's the part that bothers me." She could hear how much she sounded like a textbook, and she hated it, but she couldn't find a softer way to say something true. He didn't argue. He picked up the stack of unprinted surveys, turned them over, and began writing a new question on the blank backs in pencil, crossing out and rewriting, slower than she had ever seen him work.

They ran the second version through the afternoon, and it answered differently, less neatly, more "it depends" scrawled in margins where there was no box for it. By closing time they had fifty-two responses to one question and thirty-one to another, and Kaitlyn no longer knew which stack told her less. Charles-Antoine leaned against the doorframe eating a vending-machine sandwich and offered, through it, a piece of casuistry so ornate, an argument that both versions were true if you averaged them, that even he gave it up halfway through laughing at himself.

Ms. Gupta began sealing the ballot boxes under the anachronistic brass lamps that hung from the hall's high ceiling, and the last voters were ushered out into the blue evening. Lucas held up his clipboard. "So what do we say we found out?" he asked.

Kaitlyn looked down the empty hall, at the tables, the taped arrows on the floor, the two uneven stacks in her bag. "That we asked better the second time," she said, "and I still can't tell you by how much."

Lucas zipped his jacket. "Put that on the summary sheet, then."

She did, in pencil, under the number.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
Ryder arrived at the Aquatic Center at 7:40 in the morning with his swimsuit under his jeans and a birth certificate folded into his back pocket like a bet he wasn't sure he'd won. The pool lay flat and green under the skylights, the water so still it looked solid, a diaphanous blue rectangle with the lane lines visible beneath like veins. He had wanted this job for one reason, which he had not said out loud to anyone: his mother's hours at the hospital had been cut, and the gap in the household had begun to presage things, small curtailments, a phone plan quietly dropped to a cheaper tier, that he intended to fill before anyone asked him to.

"First day?" the cashier said, not looking up from a binder.

"Orientation," Ryder said. "Lifeguard."

She handed him a clipboard. "Fill these out. There's coffee by the lost and found."

He carried the clipboard to a bench by the deep end and sat down and discovered, within the first page, that he had no idea what he was looking at. The form was numbered I-9, and the first half of it, labeled Section 1, wanted his address, his citizenship box checked, his signature. Below it sat Section 2, which was blank and stamped with the words Employer. He read the fine print twice. It said every new employee had to complete Section 1 no later than the first day of paid work, and that today, apparently, counted.

A girl with wet hair pulled into a bun dropped onto the bench beside him. She had a whistle already around her neck, which meant she'd been through this. "I'm Averie," she said. "You're the Saturday guy?" He said he was. She pointed at his clipboard. "They give you that thing the second you walk in, right? No warning, nothing. Nobody tells you it exists until it's in your hands."

"I don't even know what it's for," Ryder said.

"Proves you're you," she said. "That you can legally work here. You do your half, they do theirs." She was reading over his shoulder, ostensibly to be helpful, actually to check whether he'd checked the same box she had. He had. She seemed to relax.

What Averie could not see, from her angle on the bench, was the phone in Ryder's hand under the clipboard, where his mother had texted him at 7:52. He read it while pretending to study the form. "Found your social security card in the folder with the tax stuff. Left it on the kitchen table. You didn't need it today did you?" He typed back, slowly, with one thumb: "Only for the form. They need it for I-9." Then, after a pause: "It's fine. I'll bring it tomorrow before my shift." His mother replied with a single thumbs up, then a second message: "Don't let them make you work before you sign anything. Know your rights." He didn't tell her the form's fine print had already told him that himself, that nothing about the arrangement was allowed to start, not paid, not officially, until his half of the paper was finished. He put the phone away and checked his boxes and signed his name with the cheap pen, and his signature came out smaller than he meant it to.

Averie watched the new boy sign. She had been through four orientations herself, counting the one where she'd been sent home for forgetting her social security card, and she had developed, in that time, a private phenomenology of first days, a way of cataloguing how each newcomer's nervousness showed itself. Some talked too much. Some went silent. This one signed his name like he was apologizing for the ink. When he turned the clipboard over to look at the back, she saw him pause at the fine print, and she remembered doing exactly that, alone, nobody explaining, the rules of being an employee arriving all at once like weather.

"Did you finish Section 1?" the head lifeguard called from across the deck, walking toward them with the binder.

"Just now," Ryder said.

"Good. Because today's a paid day." The head lifeguard took the clipboard, glanced at the signature, and moved on without ceremony.

Ms. Munro, the facility manager, appeared at the bench a minute later with two shirts folded over her arm, red and white, LIFEGUARD printed across the chest in block letters. She held one out to each of them. Averie took hers and was already pulling it on over her suit, and the whistle at her throat caught the morning light. Ryder stood up. He peeled off his jeans down to his swimsuit right there on the deck, wadded them onto the bench, and tugged the shirt over his head, and when his face came through the collar his mother's phone buzzed once more in the pocket of his folded jeans, unread.

"Deep end first," Averie said, already walking. "You take the right chair."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
The laminated schedule was taped to the chain-link fence by the shallow end, and Jake read it three times before he understood that it had nothing to do with him. It listed the pool's hours, the swim club's hours, and a note that said the club's season plan was posted on the bulletin board inside. He had come to the community pool every morning that week to swim laps before his tryouts in August, and by Thursday his shoulders burned when he raised his arms to towel his hair.

Keagan was already in the water when Jake arrived on Friday, doing sprints against the clock on the wall, and he stayed in after Jake left. On Saturday Keagan was there again, gray-faced by eleven, pulling himself out at the ladder with his arms shaking. "Twelve days straight," he said, lying flat on the hot concrete. "If I miss a day I'll lose everything."

Jake sat down beside him with his clipboard, the one his mother had bought him when he said he was serious this year. So far it held only a grid with seven columns and the word "SWIM" written in every square. "My shoulder hurts," he said.

"Good," Keagan said, eyes closed. "That's it working."

Jake wasn't sure. That was the problem with Keagan's way of thinking, that pain could be reified into proof of progress, as if soreness were a thing you could hold up and count. But Jake's own grid seemed almost equally dumb, the same word seven times, no thought in it at all. He had wanted to plan like a real athlete, and instead he had produced something a child could have made.

Inside, near the vending machines, the bulletin board held the club's season plan, and Jake stopped in front of it with his clipboard under his arm. The page was divided into blocks with labels: preparation, competition, transition. Inside the blocks were smaller blocks. At the bottom, a lifeguard he knew as Ms. Wright was refilling the first-aid kit, and she saw him squinting at the page.

"You want to read that? Take it down, then, you're fogging the glass."

He lifted the clear sheet out of its pins. Under the smallest blocks, in handwriting, was a single word: microcycle. Next to it, someone had drawn an arrow to a note that said one week. The whole season was cut into cycles, and the cycles into smaller ones, and these smallest ones ran about one week each. Each microcycle had hard days and light days and a day marked "rest" in red pen, actually written in, like it was part of the training and not the absence of it.

"Coaches call this a microcycle," Jake said, mostly to himself, his finger on the word.

"Sure," Ms. Wright said, snapping the kit shut. "That's the week. The season's the big one. Anyway, don't swim tired, that's how people drown, and it's a pain for me." She walked off toward the deep end, irascible about it, as she was about everything, but Jake barely noticed. He was copying the shape of the smallest block onto his clipboard: two hard days, a light day, a hard day, a light day, then rest. Warm-ups were written at the top of every single day, even the rest day, which had a ten-minute stretch listed beside the red word.

Outside, he found Keagan still lying on the concrete. Jake held the clipboard where he could see it. "You're swimming twelve days straight," he said. "The club team doesn't do that. Their whole season is divided into cycles, and the smallest one, the week, has a rest day built in. The coaches plan it."

Keagan sat up slowly. "So?"

"So if you don't rest, you're not training harder than them. You're training worse than them." Jake wasn't sure that was exactly true. Maybe Keagan's body was different, maybe rest was a disincentive for someone with tryouts five weeks away, and Jake could admit to himself that he didn't know. But the red pen on the club's plan looked like a decision made by people who knew something, and Jake's grid of seven identical days looked like nothing.

"I'm coming tomorrow anyway," Keagan said, standing, picking up his towel. "But maybe just the warm-up and some kicks."

"Get here at nine," Jake said, and wrote it in the Saturday box, in the space below the word SWIM, which he then crossed out and replaced with the warm-up length, the drill set, and, in the last box of the week, in red pen borrowed from the sign-in desk, one word: rest.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
story:
The last Tuesday of October, Madeline's grandfather had the news on with the volume too high, which was how most of his opinions arrived. She had come to his house to write a civics essay on how different democracies choose and fire their leaders, mostly because his kitchen had better light than her bedroom and nobody there asked her about college applications every eleven minutes.

Her grandmother was at the table doing the crossword, pencil held like a surgical instrument. "Seven letters," she said, "roundabout way of saying something."

"Circumlocution," Madeline said, and then wrote it in for her, because her grandmother's cursive was beautiful and her spelling was a matter of faith rather than record.

On the television, a crowd outside some parliament building was shouting at a man in a suit. Her grandfather shook his head at the man the way he shook his head at weather. "That one," he said. "He'll be gone by Christmas, you watch. His own people will do it." He seemed to find this satisfying in a way Madeline couldn't quite locate. He hated the man, clearly, wanted him gone, and yet admired the machinery that would remove him, the way you might admire a well-made trap even as you hated the rat.

Her phone buzzed. It was Zayan, who was doing the same essay and had chosen, characteristically, to begin his research by asking her. "quick question," his message said. "why does england have a king AND a prime minister. isn't that two bosses. this feels like two bosses."

Madeline typed back "one sec" and then sat there, because she realized she'd been skimming past exactly this for an hour. She had a page of notes about elections and no confidence votes, and the top of the page had a diagram she'd copied from a website without really reading it: two boxes for the parliamentary countries, one box for the United States.

She looked at the television again. The shouting man in the suit. Then a clip of the King, earlier that week, cutting a ribbon somewhere, smiling at a child holding a wilted bouquet. Nobody had shouted at him.

"Grandpa," she said, "when the King visits Canada, who's actually in charge?"

"The Prime Minister, obviously." He said it the way you'd say water is wet. Then, sensing a trap, he added, "The King's the head of state. He opens things. He signs things. The Prime Minister runs things. That's the whole arrangement. Keeps the flag out of the fistfight." He went back to the news, the transaction complete, unaware he had just handed her the spine of her essay.

She wrote it out for Zayan in three messages, testing it as she went. In a lot of parliamentary systems, the head of state is one job, a monarch or a ceremonial president, and the head of government is a different job, the one who actually governs and takes the shouting. In the United States, the president is both. Both hats, one head. Zayan replied with a single thumbs-up and then, a minute later, "wait so americans shout at their flag AND their boss at the same time?" which was not how she'd have put it, but wasn't wrong either.

It was the word both that made her sit back. She'd spent the evening thinking the American system was simpler, one person, one office, cleaner. Now that seemed less like simplicity and more like concentration. Her grandfather could vilify the Prime Minister all he wanted, loudly, at volume, and it cost him nothing, because the thing he actually revered was never in the fistfight. The shouting was pointed at a man who could be replaced by Christmas. Americans, as far as she could tell, had no such arrangement; the office and the man wore the same face, which explained a lot of the cable news she'd grown up thinking was normal.

Whether one was better was the question the essay asked, and it was the question she couldn't answer, and she suspected the assignment knew that. She had evidence for both sides and, worse, the sides weren't even opposite, exactly. She wrote a paragraph arguing that separating the roles made ordinary politics uglier and safer at once, then read it back and crossed out the last sentence, because she'd drifted into asserting more than she knew. What stayed certain: the arrangements were different, the American president held both jobs, and her grandfather's news would outlive several Prime Ministers.

She was still editing when her grandmother leaned over her shoulder, read the top line of the essay, and tapped it once with the pencil.

"Is any of this germane to the crossword," she said, "or are you just showing off?"

"It's germane," Madeline said. "Seven down. Second letter's a U."

Her grandmother wrote it in without checking, which was, Madeline thought, an act of government in itself, and turned the page.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story 'The Tell-Tale Heart', the narrator insists he is not mad while describing how he murdered an old man.
story:
Clara had claimed the table by the periodicals at 3:15, which she considered an act of strategy rather than desperation, and by 3:40 she had written the words Unreliable Narrator at the top of a page and then decorated the margin around them with a small vine. Ms. Hassan passed behind her with a cart of returns and said nothing, which Clara chose to interpret as approval.

The essay was due Thursday. The novel was due Thursday too, in the sense that she was supposed to have finished it by Tuesday and had instead read forty pages and the summary of the rest, a summary she already regretted trusting because it had described the ending as ambiguous in a tone that suggested the summarizer had also not read it. The problem, as she understood it from the prompt, was that she had to explain how the narrator's point of view shaped the reader's trust, and she did not yet have a position, only a feeling that she was being manipulated by someone she couldn't see.

Myles arrived at four with a bag of vending machine pretzels and the confidence of someone who had finished the book. "He's not lying," Myles said, sitting down uninvited. "He's remembering wrong. There's a difference."

"Is there?" Clara said. "For the reader, I mean. Does the reader experience the difference?"

Myles gesticulated with a pretzel, scattering salt across her vine. "Of course. A liar you distrust. Someone who's remembering wrong, you distrust them and feel sorry for them. That's two different books."

That was, annoyingly, better than anything she'd written. Clara copied it down under the vine, and Myles pretended not to notice, and both of them pretended that the pretzel salt wasn't a problem, and then Kira dropped her bag on the table and said she'd found something in the Poe section while avoiding her own essay, which was on phenotype ratios, an assignment she described as "punishment for choosing biology."

She held up a thin collection, open to a page she'd already marked with a receipt. "This one," she said. "1843. 'The Tell-Tale Heart.' Read the first paragraph."

Clara read it. The narrator was insisting, before anything had even happened, that he was not mad, that the disease had only sharpened his senses, that he could hear everything in heaven and earth and many things in hell. Then he described, in the same calm voice, how he had murdered an old man. Clara read it twice. "He murdered an old man," she said. "And he opens by telling us he's sane."

Myles leaned over. "So the protests are the problem. If he'd just told the story, you'd believe the story. He tells you he's not mad, and that's the exact thing that makes you doubt him."

"That's backwards," Clara said. "That's completely backwards and I believe it." She underlined it. Somewhere behind the underlining, a position was forming: it wasn't that the reader trusted the narrator and then discovered reasons not to. It was that the point of view built the doubt in from the first line, that the narrator's need to be believed was itself the evidence against him. She wasn't sure it held for her novel's narrator, who never insisted on anything, and she wrote that uncertainty in the margin in smaller letters, the way she stored things she intended to think about later.

Ms. Hassan stopped at the table on her way to the circulation desk. "Finding it?" she asked, and Clara said yes before she could decide whether yes was accurate, and Ms. Hassan looked at the Poe collection lying open among the salt and said, "That's where I'd start too," and moved on without explaining anything, which was, Clara thought, the entire method.

At home that night, Clara got a message from Kira, sent at 10:52:

"ok update. spent an hour on the ear. the whole thing is about an eye but I keep typing ear. anyway I looked him up and people argue about whether the narrator is mad or just guilty, like it's a real question with an answer. also my bio essay is due tomorrow not Thursday, which I have just learned, so I am now the unreliable narrator of my own life. how's the position coming"

Clara typed "solidifying" and then deleted it, because it wasn't, exactly. It was more that she had two ideas, Myles's liar-versus-rememberer distinction and her own backwards-protest thing, and they pulled against each other, and the honest version of her essay would have to hold both and admit where they didn't fit together. The narrator of her novel never protested his sanity, and yet Clara distrusted him anyway, which meant the Poe mechanism wasn't the whole mechanism, only one mechanism, and a perspicacious reader, she wrote, and then crossed out perspicacious because it sounded like showing off, would want to know what the other mechanism was. She crossed it out and then wrote it again in the margin, smaller.

She got eleven hundred words in, deleted four hundred of them, and at midnight opened the biology textbook Kira had left in her bag by mistake, because Kira's essay was due tomorrow and Kira had gone to bed. The phenotype chapter began with a picture of two mice that looked nothing like their parents, and Clara read the caption twice and thought, unhelpfully, that it was like a narrator: what you saw wasn't what was underneath, and the underneath kept doing things to the surface without announcing itself.

At 12:41 she sent Kira a photo of the marked-up chapter with the caption "your book lives," and then, because it was late and the position still had a hole in it the size of a narrator who never once said trust me, she sent a second message: "not avoiding the essay. just doing this first."

She read the message back. Then she read it again, out loud, in her own voice, hearing exactly how it sounded, and put the phone face down on the textbook, where it buzzed once against the picture of the mice.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The 4:15 bus took the long way through the more cosmopolitan end of Fairview, past the pho place and the Polish bakery and the shop that sold both prom dresses and fishing rods, and by the time it reached the school Evan had usually finished half his chemistry homework. Today he got no further than the word enthalpy, which he copied into his notebook twice and then stared at, because the seat behind him held Dereck, and the thing Evan had to say to Dereck felt heavier than any quantity of heat absorbed at constant pressure.

It had started at Monday's practice, which Dereck had missed, and again on Wednesday, which he had also missed, and the coach had pulled Evan aside afterward with the flat tone she used when she was handing him something unpleasant to carry. You're captain next term, she'd said. Tell him what that costs the relay. Then she'd walked off to blow her whistle at the freshmen, leaving Evan holding the sentence like a live wire.

"You're doing the staring-at-the-window thing," said Averie, dropping into the seat across the aisle with a paperback whose cover showed two overlapping hearts. "It's very cosmopolitan of you. Brooding on public transit."

"I'm not brooding. I'm thinking about enthalpy."

"You don't know what enthalpy is."

"That's why I'm thinking about it." He tapped her book. "What's that, anyway?"

"Psych elective. We have to read it by Friday." She flipped it around. "It's mostly about couples, but Mr. Wu says the same rules work for teams, roommates, anybody. There's this psychologist, Gottman, and he says the difference between a complaint and a criticism is huge. A complaint goes after the behavior. A criticism goes after the person."

"Those sound the same."

"They're not. 'You missed practice twice' is a complaint. 'You always mess up' is a criticism." She paused, seeming to hear herself. "Basically the whole book."

Evan looked at the window again, but differently now. Because the sentence he'd been rehearsing for two days, the one that went you never take this seriously, Derek, you're lazy, you're going to cost us counties, was suddenly visible to him in cross-section, like a diagram in the chem textbook, and what he saw inside it was not great.

"Wait," he said. "How specific does the complaint have to be?"

Averie shrugged. "Specific enough that they can actually do something about it, I think. Why, who are you complaining at?"

Dereck leaned over the seat back before Evan could demur. "If this is about practice, I already know. My mom works nights now, somebody has to pick up my sister."

The bus hissed to a stop outside the bakery and two third-graders clattered down the steps. Evan had a choice, and he could feel it, the old sentence still fully loaded and ready, easy, satisfying, aimed at Dereck's whole self. He let it pass.

"You missed practice Monday and Wednesday," he said. "That's it. That's all I've got. What happened?"

"What I said. Sister pickup."

"Okay. Can you tell the coach that directly? Because she told me to deal with it, and if she knows, she can move your warmup slot or something. She's not actually a monster, she just plays one with a whistle." Dereck didn't answer right away, so Evan kept going, quieter. "I was going to say something worse, by the way. Before Averie explained the difference, I had this whole speech about how you never take it seriously. Which, looking at it now, wasn't even true. You take it seriously, you just have a sister."

Dereck was quiet for another half block. "You had a whole speech prepared?"

"Bullet points. I rehearsed it at my locker."

"You rehearsed yelling at me?"

"I rehearsed a leadership conversation," Evan said, and Averie laughed so hard she dropped the book on the floor.

Dereck reached down, picked it up, and looked at the two hearts on the cover with deep suspicion. "If I read the couples book, does that mean I get to be captain too?"

"No, it means you text the coach tonight. Two missed practices, one sister, one solution. I'm not doing it for you, I'm just not yelling at you while you don't."

"I never asked you not to yell at me."

"Consider it a bonus." Evan turned back to his notebook, where enthalpy sat waiting, still undefined but no longer the hardest problem of the afternoon. Behind him he heard Dereck's phone camera click, photographing the page Averie held up for him, and then the small decisive sound of him beginning to type.

"Hey," Dereck said, halfway through the message. "What's enthalpy?"

"Heat absorbed at constant pressure," said Averie.

"So it's like feelings," Dereck said, "but scientific."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
Anthony had chosen the fat copy of Jane Eyre on purpose, because the spine was cracked and someone had written in the margins, and he thought a stranger's handwriting might tell him what to think. He had until Friday to write six hundred words applying a Marxist critical lens to one chapter, and so far his lens was fogged. He spread the book open on the study table by the window, third floor of the public library, where the radiators clanked like a small imprisoned animal.

"Chapter four," said Anais, dropping into the chair across from him. "That's the one you're doing?" She was working on the same assignment for a different class period, which was either lucky or dangerous, depending on who copied whom. "Mr. Tehrani says a Marxist reading asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible. You look for the people the novel only mentions in passing."

"Like the servants," Anthony said.

"Like the servants." Diego arrived with three cookies balanced on a napkin, one of which he set in front of Anthony like an offering. "I've been here forty minutes and I've read one paragraph and two vending machine nutrition labels. I'm calling that a net gain for the people."

They started counting. Anthony went line by line through the chapter with a pencil, making a small tally in the margin beside his own notes, though he felt vaguely guilty putting his marks next to the stranger's, whose cramped ink said things like "the fire is not hers" and "who cooked this." Every time a servant was named, he drew one line. Every time a servant actually spoke, he drew a circle. By the time the radiator had clanked through what felt like an hour, he had two lines and no circles. The named servants, when they appeared at all, carried trays, stoked fires, and vanished. Nobody working in that house said a single word in the entire chapter, while upstairs people delivered speeches about their feelings.

"Two names, zero lines of dialogue," Anthony said. "The whole chapter runs on invisible work."

Diego leaned over, gesticulating with his cookie as though it were a pointer. "You could literally write that sentence down and go home. Sentence, cookie, home."

"It's not a sentence yet. It's a tally." But Anthony copied it onto the back of his hand anyway.

Then Anais, reading over his shoulder, went quiet in a way he had learned to notice. "Did you write 'who cooked this' in the margin?"

"No. It was already in the book." He turned the pages back. There were notes all through it, in the same cramped ink, some of them sharper than anything Anthony felt capable of thinking. One said, "The comfort is an amalgam of someone else's hours." He did not know all the words in it, but he knew it was good, and he knew it was not his, and he sat for a moment with the uncomfortable feeling of wanting something he had not earned.

"Anthony," Anais said, slowly, "if you use a stranger's notes, that's not applying a lens. That's borrowing someone's eyes."

"Notes in a library book aren't a person's essay. They're just there. Like weather." He heard how it sounded even as he said it. He took out his phone and typed a message to Mr. Tehrani, who was, improbably, also the librarian on Saturdays and answered library emails from the reference desk: found a used copy with extensive margin notes, chapter four, Jane Eyre. Is using them plagiarism or luck? He watched the three dots appear, disappear, and appear again, and the pause before the answer felt longer than it probably was.

The reply came while Diego was arguing that any assignment you could finish in one afternoon could not be a serious assignment, and while Anais was incisive about exactly how wrong he was, in a single sentence Diego did not recover from for the rest of the afternoon. Anthony read the message twice.

The handwriting in that copy is mine, Mr. Tehrani wrote. First year of university. I was twenty and certain of everything except the essay, which I got a B minus on. The notes are a record of one reader's attempt, not an authority. Use them as a conversation, not a script, and cite the edition, not me. Also, the tally is the right instinct. Trust the tally.

Anthony put the phone face down on the table. "The margin notes are Mr. Tehrani's," he said. "From college. He got a B minus."

Diego laughed so suddenly that a crumb went somewhere it should not have, and he had to spend a while recovering. "Your teacher's ghost has been haunting your book."

"He's not a ghost. He's downstairs at the reference desk." Anthony looked at the ink again, at who cooked this, and found it looked different now, less like a gift and more like somebody else's honest confusion, preserved. He wrote his first real sentence at the top of a blank page: In chapter four the servants are named twice and never speak, and the comfort of the house depends on them anyway. It was his own tally and it was true whether or not anyone had ever written it before.

Anais read it over his shoulder and nodded once, which was more than she gave most sentences. Then she leaned past him and tapped the window. Down on the front steps of the library, Mr. Tehrani was carrying a crate of returned books in through the doors, setting it down, and going back for another one.

"Whose labour," Diego said, pointing at him with the last cookie.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
The living room had been rearranged for the semifinal, the couch dragged closer to the television, folding chairs borrowed from the kitchen, a bowl of pistachios balanced on the armrest where nobody could knock it over. Gabrielle had the spot on the floor with her back against the coffee table, which was the worst seat and, she had decided weeks ago, the one she liked most, because from there she could see everyone's faces instead of only the screen. Her father shouted at the referee. Aikam, who had come over with a bag of sour candies and opinions about the back line, leaned forward every time the ball crossed midfield.

In the eighty-eighth minute, with the score still level, the striker wheeled away from his marker and drove a shot inside the far post. The room erupted. Her father was on his feet, Manraj was laughing the high startled laugh he saved for moments like this, and even Ms. Kelly from next door, who had let herself in through the back door with a plate of squares and had watched the whole match with polite bafflement, clapped her hands together twice.

Then the striker stopped celebrating. He was looking at the linesman, and the linesman was looking at nothing, and in the corner of the screen a small box appeared with three white letters. The room went quiet so completely that Gabrielle could hear the refrigerator humming in the kitchen.

"It's the review," Aikam said. "The video review. They're checking the goal."

Manraj groaned and dropped back into his chair. "This is what's ruined football. You score, you celebrate, and then you stand around for two minutes while somebody in a room decides whether joy is allowed."

"Goals, penalties, red cards," Aikam said, counting on his fingers. "And if they booked the wrong player. That's all it can look at." He had read an article about it, he admitted, mostly because the article had claimed broadcasters were trying to monetize the suspense, cutting to the referee's face during the wait and selling that silence to advertisers. He thought this was cynical. He also thought it was probably true.

Ms. Kelly asked, in the tone of someone being careful with new vocabulary, "This is new? They didn't have it before?"

"This World Cup is the first one," Gabrielle said, and heard herself say it with more certainty than she felt. "The first with the video referees. In Russia." She had looked it up after the group stage, after a penalty had been given in a match she'd watched alone and she had wanted to know whether her sense of injustice had any procedure behind it. The system could review four things, the site had said, and she had memorized them the way she memorized anything she planned to argue about: goals, penalties, direct red cards, and cases of mistaken identity, which was the one that fascinated her, the idea that a referee could confuse one player with another in the middle of a crowded penalty area and that somewhere a camera had kept better track.

On the screen the referee stood with his hand against his ear, listening to somebody Gabrielle could not see. The replays came in strips: the pass that started the move, clearly onside; the shoulder-to-shoulder contact at the edge of the box, ambiguous from one angle and clean from another; then, at last, a thread of space between the striker's boot and the last defender's knee, held on the line, measured, held again. Manraj said that football was a game of moments and that stretching a moment until it dried out killed what the moment was for. Aikam said that a goal that shouldn't count wasn't a moment at all, it was a mistake wearing a moment's clothes. They had had versions of this argument three times this tournament, and it had a ritual quality now, almost affectionate, less like disagreement than mutualism, each of them protecting the other from being entirely right.

Gabrielle listened to both of them and found, to her own mild surprise, that she could not pick a side, or rather that she could pick both and hold them at once. The review was fair and the review was cold, and the strange thing was that these weren't opposing claims but the same claim turned toward and away from the light. What she couldn't settle, even privately, was whether fairness was worth what it cost the celebrating, whether a correct goal that arrived like a verdict was better than a wrong one that arrived like a gift. She suspected the answer depended on which team you supported, and she suspected that was exactly why nobody in the room would admit it.

The referee drew a rectangle in the air with his hands, and the goal stood. Her father's shout rattled the pistachio bowl, Manraj was up apologizing to nobody for nothing, and Ms. Kelly asked, over the noise, whether the referee had made the decision himself or someone had told him what to see. Gabrielle opened her mouth, realized she did not know, and closed it again.

"That," she said, "is the part they don't show you."

Aikam tossed her a sour candy, underhand, and she caught it without looking away from the screen as the striker, at last, was allowed to finish celebrating.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1791, says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech.
story:
The mock court packet lay open on the library table between Kate and Avery, forty pages of a real Supreme Court case about a student suspended for a banner she had unfurled at a school event. Their assignment, unusual and slightly cruel, was to argue both sides, petitioner in the morning, respondent in the afternoon, and to believe each one enough to survive questions. Kate read the opening line aloud before either of them had chosen anything: "The First Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1791, says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech." She said it twice, slowly the second time, because the words felt older and stranger in her mouth than they had in any textbook.

"That's it?" Avery said. "That's the whole thing we're building on?"

"That's the whole thing," Kate said. "Congress shall make no law." She tapped the page. "It doesn't say schools. It doesn't say principals. It says Congress."

Avery, saturnine in the late afternoon light, folded her arms and observed that this was exactly the problem. A school principal is not Congress, so maybe the amendment simply does not reach him, the way a leash law does not reach a cat. Kate pushed back, saying the courts had never read it that narrowly, that the principle had to underpin every government actor or it underpinned nothing. They argued for twenty minutes without resolving anything, which was, she realized later, the point of the assignment.

That night she sat on her bedroom floor with the banner case beside a second one Mr. Clarke had slipped into her folder after class, unrequested. He had said only, "You'll want the counterweight," and walked away, hands in his pockets, leaving her to find it herself. The counterweight was a case about a school that had censored a newspaper, and the Court had let the school do it. Kate read until eleven, and the two decisions sat in her mind like two people describing the same room from opposite doors.

She remembered, without wanting to, a thing from ninth grade: a boy in her English class who had made a joke about her freckles in front of everyone, and how she had defended him to the teacher on free speech grounds, young and righteous, and how she had gone home and cried anyway. At the time she had thought those two facts cancelled each other out. Now she suspected they did not cancel; they just coexisted, the way the amendment and the school's authority coexisted, neither one willing to leave the room.

The next morning she and Avery rehearsed in the empty chemistry lab, Kate standing at the fume hood as if it were the bench of justices. "Petitioner," Avery intoned, playing the judge with theatrical gravity, "does the First Amendment protect a banner calling for, quote, the overthrow of money itself?"

"It protects the message," Kate said, "even a silly one. Money in politics has turned governance toward plutocracy, and the student's banner said so. Speech about power is the speech the amendment was written for."

"Then you may sit," Avery said. "And rise for the other side."

Kate stood again, and the strange thing was that the second argument came out just as strongly, maybe more so. Schools, she said, are not the public square; they are a place where fourteen-year-olds are compelled by law to sit together for seven hours, and a principal has to keep that room workable. Congress shall make no law, she conceded, but a principal is not Congress, and the Court has always known that. She heard herself and thought, not for the first time, that certainty felt different depending on which door you entered the room from.

Mr. Clarke watched the final run-through from the back of the auditorium, leaning against the folded bleachers, and afterward he asked her only one question: "Which one do you actually believe?" Kate stood in the aisle with her notes still in her hand. She thought of the freckles boy, of the banner, of the chemistry lab where both arguments had felt true in turn. "The speech side," she said finally. "Mostly. But I keep the other one warm." Mr. Clarke nodded once and began stacking chairs.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: For US federal Direct Subsidized student loans, the government pays the interest while the student is in school; unsubsidized loans build interest during that time.
story:
The financial aid letter had been sitting in Clara's inbox since Tuesday, and she opened it now only because her mother asked twice. Two columns filled the screen: Direct Subsidized Loan, $3,500, and Direct Unsubsidized Loan, $2,000, followed by words Clara read three times without feeling them settle. At the kitchen table behind her, her mother was on the phone with the clinic, saying "antigen test" in the tone of someone who had said it many times this month, and Clara turned back to the screen as though it could be bargained with.

She texted Edouard first because Edouard had a spreadsheet for everything. "Did your letter have both kinds of loans?" He called instead of texting, voluble as always, telling her about his cousin's debt and his uncle's opinions before she could say what she actually wanted to know. "I took the subsidized," he said finally. "The other one builds interest while you're still in school. The subsidized one doesn't. The government pays the interest on it while you're enrolled." He said it like a weather report, no drama, and Clara wrote both sentences in her notebook because she did not trust her memory with money.

She opened the federal aid page anyway and confirmed it herself, scrolling past paragraphs of caveats. While she was in school, the unsubsidized loan would quietly grow, the borrowed amount detaching from the number on the letter, becoming something larger before she ever made a payment. The subsidized loan would sit still, held at its original size. She thought of it as one door staying where it was and the other one drifting down the hall while you slept, which was not accurate, but it helped.

The problem was that the two together did not cover what the college expected her family to pay. Her mother came off the phone and stood behind her, reading over her shoulder, one hand resting on the chair back the way she did when she wanted to appear calmer than she was. "Can you take more of the good kind?" her mother asked, and Clara had to say no, that the amounts were fixed, that the letter offered what it offered. Her mother nodded and went to start dinner, and Clara heard her chopping something slowly, evenly, as if the rhythm itself were a budget.

Tegan came over at seven with her own letter folded in her back pocket, having decided the printout made things more real. They sat shoulder to shoulder at the computer, and Clara explained what she had learned, pointing at the screen. "So the subsidized one is the one where nothing grows while I'm in school," Tegan said, testing it, "and the unsubsidized one starts costing more right away." Clara confirmed it and felt the small pleasure of teaching something she had owned for only four hours. Tegan, who had planned to work a gap year and pay cash, was quiet for a while. "My mom wants me to just go now," she said, which was not about loans at all, and Clara understood that they had stopped talking about the letter.

Here was where Clara's two ways of thinking collided. One voice, her father's, said debt was debt and borrowing was a trap dressed in paperwork; the other, Edouard's spreadsheet voice, said some debt was structured to emancipate you, to buy the education that made the borrowing back. She had always assumed the first voice was the moral one.
