Sitting at the screen, she changed her mind, though not completely, because the second voice still required her to bet on a future self who would earn enough to pay, and no letter could promise that. She accepted both loans. Then, before she could second-guess, she opened her savings account page and looked at the interest rate, which was small and which she had never once thought about, and set up an automatic transfer of forty dollars a month. If interest worked while you weren't watching, she wanted it working for her somewhere.

Ms. Chatterjee from next door knocked at eight with a covered dish, saying she'd made too much dal and heard from Clara's mother about the college news. She asked careful questions and did not give advice, which Clara appreciated more than she could say, except once at the door when she paused and said, "My father paid off his loan for eleven years. Check which kind you have before you sign anything." Clara told her she had, twice. Ms. Chatterjee smiled and said, "Then you're ahead of me at your age."

Later that night Clara turned off the lamp but left the computer screen glowing, the acceptance page still open, her name already typed into the box at the bottom. She read the summary line once more: subsidized, unsubsidized, the difference between them now a fact she could hold. Then she clicked submit, and the screen went white and asked her to wait.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: Bigger samples help less than people expect: doubling a random sample from 1,000 to 2,000 people shrinks the margin of error by only about one percentage point.
story:
The line at the recreation centre stretched past the folding tables and out beneath the dour grey awning, and Alexandra stood at its end holding a clipboard she did not entirely understand. Ciara had signed them up for exit polling that morning, thrusting the clipboard at her outside the school gates before Alexandra could invent an excuse. "Six hundred responses," Ciara had said, "and the news will call it before nine." Now the voters shuffled forward in wet coats, and Alexandra's task was simpler than the morning's promise: ask, tally, thank.

She had learned the sample's arithmetic two nights earlier, at her kitchen table, arguing with her mother about whether the polls could be trusted. Her mother dichotomized the whole business into liars and truth-tellers and placed every pollster firmly in the first camp. Alexandra, who liked to sort things, had spent an hour building a small taxonomy of the arguments instead: the ones about who was asked, the ones about who answered, the ones about how many. The last category had surprised her. She had looked up what a margin of error actually meant, expecting it to shrink in proportion to effort, and found that it did not.

By mid-morning she had one hundred and eleven tallies, and her hand ached. Ciara arrived at noon with sandwiches and a plan, flushed from the phone bank where she had been calling likely voters all week. "I got the coordinator to say maybe," Ciara said, wedging herself onto the bench beside Alexandra. "If we double the calls, from a thousand to two thousand, the poll gets accurate. That's how it works, right? Double the people, double the certainty."

Alexandra peeled the wax paper off her sandwich slowly. She thought of the kitchen table, of her own certainty that evening, and of how she had been wrong in a way she still found faintly humiliating. "That's what I thought too," she said. "I looked it up. Doubling the sample from a thousand to two thousand only shrinks the margin of error by about one percentage point. That's all you get."

Ciara stared at the line of voters as though they had personally betrayed her. "One point? For a thousand extra calls?"

"One point." Alexandra watched a man in a green raincoat make his mark and slide his ballot into the box. "I checked it twice because I didn't believe it."

Ms. Owusu, who taught statistics at the college and had lived three doors down from Alexandra since she was small, came through the doors at half past one and stopped at their table on her way out. She was unhurried, unhappily dressed for the rain, and clearly amused to find Alexandra holding a clipboard. "And how goes the science of guessing?" she asked.

Ciara appealed to her at once, laying out the whole scheme, the thousand calls and the thousand more, and Alexandra watched Ms. Owusu's face for the verdict. "She's not wrong that more is better," Ms. Owusu said, nodding toward Alexandra. "Only wrong about how much better, if she got the direction right." She took a leaflet from the stack, folded it into her coat pocket, and did not stay to settle the matter, which Alexandra understood was its own kind of teaching.

The afternoon thinned the line. Alexandra's tallies crossed two hundred, then two hundred and fifty, and she found herself less interested in the running count than in the faces attached to it: the woman who said "you'll have me down as undecided forever" and laughed; the young man who refused, politely, twice. The poll would dichotomize all of them in the end, she thought, into red and blue columns, a tidy taxonomy that would fit on a screen and please the anchors at nine o'clock. She kept tallying anyway, because the alternative was guessing, and guessing without counting seemed worse than counting imperfectly. She was less sure than she had been at fourteen, or at least less sure in a more specific way, and she had not decided whether that was loss or gain.

At closing, Ciara sat on the table edge with her shoes dangling and the tally sheets fanned across her knees. "So I'll tell the coordinator not to bother with the extra thousand calls," she said. It was not quite a question.

"Tell her what the number is," Alexandra said. "One point. Then she can decide." She clipped the sheets together and looked out through the glass doors at the streetlights coming on along the wet pavement. Behind them, the election workers began carrying the sealed boxes toward the van, one worker steadying the last box against her hip as the doors swung open.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In a strike, employees refuse to work; in a lockout, the employer stops work by keeping employees out of the workplace.
story:
The loading dock lights were on at six in the morning, but the warehouse doors were chained, and a laminated sign fluttered against the metal: CLOSED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. Wyatt stood with his bike between his knees, reading the sign twice, then a third time, because it refused to say what it meant. His shift started at six thirty. He had been restocking shelves at Fedler Distribution since March, saving for a laptop he'd already picked out, and in six weeks of Sundays he had never once arrived to find the building dark.

"Are they on strike?" he asked the woman beside him, one of the pickers from the night crew, her hands buried in her jacket pockets.

"No, honey. We're locked out." She nodded at the sign. "We voted down their contract offer and we were ready to keep working while we bargained. They shut the doors on us. A strike is when the workers stop working. A lockout is when the company stops the workers from coming in."

Wyatt turned that over while more cars pulled into the lot. So the company had chosen this. The union had asked for a raise from sixteen dollars to eighteen, and for the freezer crews to stop being scheduled for ten-hour shifts without overtime after eight, and management had answered with chains.

Mr. Nikolaidis, who ran the shipping office and had worked at Fedler for twenty-six years, stood near the chain-link gate with a clipboard he wasn't using. He had been the one who hired Wyatt, who showed him how to wrap a pallet so it wouldn't topple in the truck, who told him on his first day that the union would take eleven dollars a month out of his cheque whether he joined or not and that he should decide for himself. Wyatt had signed the card mostly because Mr. Nikolaidis made the whole place feel like something worth belonging to. Now the old man looked smaller, standing outside a building he practically lived in.

"They can do that?" Wyatt asked him. "Just lock us out?"

"Legally? Yes." Mr. Nikolaidis tapped the clipboard against his thigh. "The labour board has rules about it, replacement workers, how notice has to be given. The union has lawyers going over it right now. The law allows the lockout and the strike both; what it doesn't allow is pretending this is nobody's decision."

Kaylee arrived at six twenty, earbuds still in, her backpack slung over one shoulder. She worked the same shift as Wyatt, scanning cartons, and she was saving for something more urgent than a laptop: her first semester's tuition deposit, due in three weeks. When she saw the sign she pulled out both earbuds at once, a small somatic jolt, her whole body registering the news before her mouth did. "Tell me this is a joke," she said. "Tell me I didn't just lose four weeks of shifts."

"I've got two thousand saved," Wyatt said. "I could lend you half."

"And when do you pay me back?" Kaylee said, which wasn't cruel, only arithmetic, and Wyatt hated that he could hear the arithmetic in his own head too, the laptop dimming in his mind like a screen dropping its brightness. He had spent months letting the job inculcate him in a simple faith: show up, work hard, the cheque clears. The lockout had broken the faith in a single morning, and something more complicated was leaking in to fill the space.

By noon a picket line had formed along the frontage road, hand-lettered signs and a folding table with a thermos. Kevin from the dock waved Wyatt over and handed him a marker. "Even the part-timers," Kevin said. "You're on the schedule, you're locked out, you're one of us." Wyatt took the marker and wrote LOCKED OUT, NOT ON STRIKE in block letters, because the distinction felt like the whole truth of the day, and he held the sign up when a truck slowed at the gate, its driver leaning out to read.

A white car from a staffing agency rolled past the pickets toward the gate, and Wyatt understood, in a cold and specific way, what the next month would look like: strangers doing his job for less money, the freezer crews running ten-hour shifts somewhere he couldn't see, and himself on a roadside with a sign, three hundred dollars poorer every week the doors stayed chained. He thought about the union's demand, eighteen dollars, and about the company's lawyers, and about how Mr. Nikolaidis had said the law permits both weapons but makes no promises about who bleeds. Kaylee stood beside him blowing into her cupped hands. "Three weeks," she said again, softer this time, and Wyatt shifted his sign to his other hand and put his arm across her shoulders while the gate swung open for the strangers' car.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Ryan had commandeered the last big table in the library's makerspace, the one by the window where the afternoon light came in sideways and made the glaze samples look like wet candy. His duffel sat on the second chair, which was a move he had learned from Sana, who guarded tables the way other people guarded secrets. He was building a set of three tiles for his grandmother's seventieth birthday, each one stamped with a word she used to say in a language he half knew: patience, patience, patience. He had chosen earthenware clay because it was the color of her kitchen floor in the old apartment, terra cotta gone soft with decades of feet.

Sana arrived with her own bag and, without asking, set a block of white clay beside his tiles. "Same firing, right?" she said, already unwrapping it. "We can share the kiln space. Ms. Berg said it runs Thursday."

Ryan looked at the white block. It was porcelain, and he knew it the way you know someone's handwriting, from months of watching Sana make thin, elegant bowls that survived where his thicker things cracked. He wanted to say yes, because sharing meant the project was half hers, and he was not sure he wanted to admit how much of the tile design he had already quietly copied from things she did. But something about the two clays sitting together bothered him, the way two keys for different locks bother you when they're on the same ring.

"I don't actually know," he said. "Yours is porcelain, right?"

"Obviously." She held up a pinch pot so thin the light passed through its wall. "It's my grandmother's whole lineage of showoff pottery. Thin walls, high fire. It's a family style."

He went to the shelf by the kiln where Ms. Berg kept the craft books nobody read, and pulled down the one with the cracked spine, the firing manual someone had donated in 1998. The pages smelled like a basement. He found a chart and read it twice, then once more, because the numbers felt like they were sliding off him.

"Okay, so," he said, coming back. "Earthenware fires below about twelve hundred degrees. Porcelain goes between about twelve hundred and fourteen hundred."

"So they're compatible," Sana said. "Twelve hundred's in both ranges. Kind of."

"That's the problem. It's kind of in one and definitely not the other." He tapped the chart. "If I fire hot enough for your porcelain, I don't even know what happens to mine. If we stay low, mine's fine and yours isn't."

Sana leaned over the book. She was quiet for a moment, which was unusual, and the quiet had a texture to it, like she was deciding whether to be annoyed or interested. "So we'd need two loads," she said. "Two firings. Ms. Berg will love that. She told me the kiln costs like a dollar an hour to run and she says it like it's a hundred."

Ms. Berg appeared with the timing of a person who monitored the room through some phenotypic instinct for teenagers near equipment. "Two loads of what?"

"Nothing," Ryan said, at the same moment Sana said, "Two loads of kiln."

Ms. Berg looked at the two clays on the table, then at the manual open on Ryan's knee, and something in her face suggested she had watched this exact misunderstanding happen before, possibly annually. "You worked that out yourselves?" she said. "Good. I'm not explaining kilns again. I explained kilns in 2004 and it nearly ended me." She straightened a jar of brushes that did not need straightening and left.

"She's a poem," Sana said.

They split the tasks. Thursday would be his earthenware, low and safe, and Friday hers, hot enough that Ms. Berg had to sign a separate form, which Sana claimed was institutional bias against porcelain and Ryan claimed was a form. He rolled out his third tile while she wedged her clay, and he noticed he was working slower now, more carefully, as though the clay had become a material with requirements instead of just dirt you argued with. Last spring he had thrown away a whole set of mugs rather than fire them, because his father had said pottery was a waste of a semester, and he had not argued, which still sat in him like a stone in a shoe. He wondered sometimes whether the throwing away had been cowardice or just a different kind of accounting, whether some things you abandon so that later you can come back with better information, or whether that was only a story you told yourself in libraries at four in the afternoon.

"I'll help you load Friday," he said. "If you want."

"If I want," Sana repeated, shaping a bowl that was already better than anything he would make this year. "You realize you're only helping because you want to see the kiln go hot."

"That's slander," he said, and it was also completely true, and she knew it, and stamped the word PATIENCE into the wet clay harder than he meant to.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
The photo arrived on her grandmother's phone at breakfast, and by evening it had migrated to the living room, where her grandmother sat with the screen tilted toward Mya like evidence in a trial. It showed a street underwater to the second story, a boat snagged on a balcony, a man on a roof holding a sign that said HELP. "Share this," her grandmother said. "People need to know what's happening in Ohio."

Mya took the phone. The caption underneath claimed the flood was three days old and rising, though the water in the picture was the flat green of a swimming pool left too long, and the light had a strange, even quality she couldn't name. She wanted to say yes, because her grandmother asked for so little, and because the picture was seismic, the kind of image that rearranged a whole city in your head. Instead she said, "Hold on," and pulled her laptop onto the couch.

She cogitated badly under pressure, she knew that about herself. So she slowed down. There was a way to check a picture, something Maja had done once when a photo of their burned-down gym turned out to be from a fire in a different state, years before. Mya couldn't remember the steps, only Maja's face when she'd said, "You can search the picture itself." She texted her: how did you do that thing with the gym picture. Then, while she waited, she saved the flood photo from her grandmother's phone and emailed it to herself.

Maja replied with two words and a screenshot. Reverse image search. The screenshot showed a search bar with a little camera icon in it, and under that, a button reading search by image. Mya clicked the camera. It offered her two doors: upload a picture, or paste a link to one. She uploaded the file. The page churned, then filled with results, and the results were not about Ohio at all.

The picture was real, that was the first thing, and she felt the small shame of having doubted it. It was real and it was old. The earliest hits were from 2015, a flood in a country her grandmother's caption never mentioned, and the same photograph had been reposted for years as various disasters, wearing various locations like costumes. Somewhere in the middle of the results a fact surfaced that Mya hadn't known, which was that this whole method had existed since 2011, when Google added search by image, and that the rest of the web had spent more than a decade pretending it didn't. Anyone could upload a picture or paste its link and see every place it appeared. The check took eleven seconds. She had spent three years sharing things without running it.

"There," her grandmother said, pointing at the screen as if Mya had proven the caption true.

"It's not Ohio," Mya said. "It's from 2015. Somewhere else entirely."

Her grandmother took off her glasses, put them back on, leaned in. "The water's real."

"The water's real. The where and the when aren't." She turned the laptop so her grandmother could see the dates marching down the page, the same rooftop, the same sign, recycled through flood after flood. Her grandmother was quiet in a way that Mya recognized as pride being reorganized from the inside, and she didn't rush it.

Boston had sent the same photo to their group chat an hour before, with three exclamation points and a chain of sad faces, and Mya had already typed "oh my god" and deleted it and typed it again. Now she copied the link to the oldest source and pasted it into the chat, then added, in a message she rewrote twice so it wouldn't sound like a lecture: "search by image, upload the pic, see where it's been." She watched the typing dots start and stop, start and stop. Boston was not a dilettante about causes, he was a believer, the first to sign and the first to mourn, and the dots kept stopping.

Her grandmother was still scrolling the results, her finger slow on the trackpad, and when she reached the bottom she said, "So who took it?" and Mya said she didn't know, that the picture could be honest and the caption a lie and both of those things could sit inside the same photo forever, and her grandmother nodded once, like a woman accepting a diagnosis. Then she picked up her phone, opened her messages, and instead of forwarding, she began to type.

In the group chat, Boston's reply finally landed: a single link, and above it, "you were right, deleting it." Mya looked at the message for a long moment, then turned the laptop toward her grandmother. "Show me the button again," her grandmother said.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator heat, the way it did in late afternoon, and Laurie had the place almost to herself: her cello, a music stand, and a wedge of crepuscular light sliding down the far wall. She was working on the Brahms, or trying to. Six weeks into her first year of serious study, she could read the notes fine; it was making them sound like anything that eluded her.

She heard the door at the back open before she saw anyone. A boy came down the aisle carrying a violin case, maybe ten years old, with the lopsided confidence of someone who had been told he was good at this and believed it. Behind him came Ms. Wilson, keys in hand.

"Laurie, this is Jaylen," Ms. Wilson said. "He's borrowing the room before his lesson. Jaylen, don't touch the light board again."

"That was one time," Jaylen said, and Laurie laughed despite herself.

She went back to the Brahms while he unpacked in the corner. Her sound was careful and small, each note read, verified, produced, like a chemistry problem where she kept checking the enthalpy values against the table because she didn't trust herself to remember. Ms. Wilson had said that to her once, actually: "You compute the notes instead of singing them." Laurie hadn't known what to do with the comment, so she had filed it away the way she filed most things, in the folder marked later.

Then Jaylen started to play, and she stopped.

He was playing the piece she was playing. Not the same part; the melody line, sweet and unbothered, with a little slide into the high note that sounded like an accident but landed exactly right. She watched his stand, which held no music. He was looking out at the empty seats, playing to them.

"How," Laurie said, when he finished. "Where's your sheet music?"

"I don't got any."

"Then how do you know the notes?"

He shrugged, as if this were a strange question. "I heard it. My grandma plays it on Sunday. I heard it a bunch of times."

"You memorized it by ear? The whole thing?" She thought of her own hours with the printed page, counting ledger lines, writing fingerings in pencil so faint her teacher could erase them. Something in her chest that felt adjacent to jealousy, but warmer, closer to exhilaration.

"Since I was little," Jaylen said. "It's the Suzuki method. My first teacher did it with me. You learn to play by ear first, before you read music. Like how you learn to talk before you learn to read."

"Wait, say that again." She had come all the way down from the stage without noticing. "Talk before read. That's actually the order? That's a whole method?"

"Suzuki," he said, slower, as though she might be a little slow. "Some Japanese guy invented it. A violin guy."

"Shinichi Suzuki," Ms. Wilson called from the sound booth, without turning around, and Laurie got the message: find out the rest yourself.

She sat on the stage edge with her cello across her knees and thought about it. She had always assumed reading music was the entrance, the toll you paid before you were allowed to sound like anything. It had never occurred to her that the order could be flipped, that sound could come first and notation after, the way speech came before spelling. And Jaylen, meanwhile, could not read a note. She'd seen him squint at her stand as he passed, the way she squinted at French menus.

"I could teach you to read," she said. "Some. If you want."

Jaylen considered this with visible suspicion. "What do I give you?"

She almost said nothing, then thought better of it. "You play the Brahms melody again and I watch your fingers. That's the trade."

He played it four times, and she watched, and by the fourth time she had stopped watching his fingers and started listening, really listening, to where he let the phrase breathe. Then she took her cello and tried the melody herself, no stand, no page, from memory of his memory. The first attempt collapsed. The second one held, wobbled, held.

Ms. Wilson came down the aisle with her keys. "Jaylen, your mother's out front."

He packed up fast. At the door he turned. "You sounded less dead that time," he said, which she decided to take as a compliment.

The wedge of light had climbed to the ceiling. Laurie looked at her stand, at the printed page with its faint pencil fingerings, and then she looked at the empty hall where the sound had gone. She left the stand where it was and started the melody again from the top.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Georges Lefebvre's 1939 book, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution, described 1789 as four revolutions: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular and peasant.
story:
Carter arrived at the library twenty minutes before the after-school writing lab closed, which he suspected was a form of self-sabotage he had chosen deliberately. His historiographical essay, due Monday, currently had a title, a thesis he no longer believed, and three paragraphs that all said the same thing in slightly different words. The prompt was straightforward enough on paper: trace how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. In practice every book he opened seemed to disagree with the last one, and he could not figure out how to organize disagreement without taking sides, which he was not yet qualified to do.

He spread his sources across the table by the window. The late light came through the blinds in flat orange stripes and lay across the pages like something the library had put there to make the scene look studious. Lindsay slid into the chair opposite him with a stack of index cards and a look of exaggerated pity.

"Still the Revolution?"

"Still the Revolution."

"You could do what Ms. Ramírez keeps saying," Lindsay said, arranging the cards into a fan. "Organize by interpretation, not by year. Like, one paragraph for the guys who thought it was a class thing, one for the guys who thought it was a disaster."

"I know what she's saying. I just don't know how to make the paragraphs hold anything. Each one turns into a list. Burke thought it was chaos, then Tocqueville thought it was continuity, then the Marxists thought it was bourgeois, then the revisionists thought the Marxists were wrong." He tapped the page. "That's not an essay, that's a receipt."

Lindsay turned her cards over one at a time without answering, which was her way of conceding the point. Down the table, Callie was copying quotations into a notebook with a mechanical pencil, and when she heard the word receipt she looked up and told him his real problem was that he kept treating 1789 as one event, which meant every interpretation looked like a rival rather than a witness to something different.

Carter started to argue and then stopped, because the objection he had been forming dissolved as he heard it. He pulled back the book he'd checked out on Monday and hadn't properly read, the thin one by Georges Lefebvre, published in 1939, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution. He flipped through it looking for the part Callie seemed to be paraphrasing without knowing it, and found it near the beginning: Lefebvre hadn't described a single revolution at all.

"He says there were four," Carter said, half to himself.

"Four of what?" Callie asked, still writing.

"Four revolutions, all in 1789. Aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular and peasant. The nobles resisting the crown, the bourgeois taking over politics, the crowds in Paris, the peasants in the countryside. Same year, same word, four different upheavals."

Lindsay leaned over the table. "So the interpretations aren't fighting. They're each looking at a different one."

"That's what it would mean." Carter felt the structure assemble itself the way a shelf does when the last bracket clicks in. He could give each paragraph a revolution to organize around, and the changes since 1800 would stop being a quarrel and become a slow shift in which upheaval people thought was the real one. He started writing in the margin of his draft, then stopped again.

"What if it's not true?" he said. "What if it's just his frame, and the people after him dismantled it? I'd be building my essay on a 1939 book that half the later scholars wrote against."

"So build it there," Callie said. "Say you're using his map of four revolutions as a way in, and say straight out that the map itself is one of the things historians have argued about. Then the uncertainty is part of the essay instead of a hole in it."

He sat with that for a moment. It was a strange relief, admitting that the ground he was standing on was itself contested ground; it felt less like weakness than like accuracy. In the margin of his opening paragraph he wrote the date 1939, then drew a line underneath it, then wrote nothing else, because the bell for closing was going to ring and he wanted to check out one more book before it did. The librarian was already moving along the shelves with a cart, reshelving the returns, and as she passed the antiquity section she paused at a shelf of bellicose-looking accounts of ancient wars, none of which he needed, and one of which he took anyway.

At the circulation desk he explained to the cashier, who was a student aide and not a librarian, that the ancient wars book was for recreational purposes and not for his French Revolution essay, and that his French Revolution essay was going to be, he thought, finally under control. He said this with some satisfaction. The aide stamped the due date, slid both books across, and told him the Lefebvre was already three days overdue.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
The sugar sat in the heavy pan like sand, white and inert, and Jeremy turned the burner to medium because that was what the recipe said, though the recipe had not mentioned what the sugar would do while it waited. It had to be dessert night, of all nights. His mother had worked doubles all week, his father had called to say he would try to make it, and Jeremy had volunteered, in the voice of someone volunteering for something smaller, to cook the whole meal in Mr. Rossi's classroom kitchen on Thursday evenings, when the room stayed open for students who signed up.

"You're staring at it like it owes you money," Hilary said. She was at the next station, chopping onions for her own project, and she kept glancing over. "It's sugar. It just sits there until it doesn't."

"Everything in cooking is like that," Cullen said from the doorway. He had come to steal leftovers, as he did every week, a tall, taciturn boy who mostly communicated by eating. He set his backpack on the counter and folded his arms. "My gran used to say you don't watch caramel, you listen to it. Then she'd burn it anyway."

Jeremy adjusted the flame lower. The sugar had begun to sweat at the edges, going glassy, and he thought about the conversation at dinner three nights ago, his mother saying his father always equivocated about whether he'd come, always left himself a way out, and his father saying nothing, which was its own kind of answer. Jeremy had promised himself he would not be like that about the meal. He would commit. He had written the menu on the whiteboard at home, four courses, no hedging.

The edges of the sugar darkened first, a pale gold spreading inward like a tide. Jeremy leaned closer.

"It's turning," Hilary said, abandoning her onions entirely.

"I know."

"Do you know when to take it off?"

He did not, exactly. He knew the number, because he had looked it up that afternoon in the food science book Mr. Rossi kept on the shelf by the door. Table sugar began to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius, and caramelization, the book had been careful to say, was the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins involved. That distinction had stuck with him. It was not like the browning of the chicken he'd made for the main course, which had the meat's own stuff in it. This was sugar alone in the pan, changing into something else by nothing but heat.

"Caramelization," he said aloud, mostly to himself. "That's what it's called. Sugar browning on its own, no proteins. Starts around 170 Celsius."

"Sounds like a disease," Cullen said.

"It's chemistry," Jeremy said, and then, because Cullen had raised an eyebrow, "Fine, it's both."

The problem was the heat itself. The recipe said medium, but the pan was dark and heavy and the classroom stove ran hot, and the gold was darkening toward amber faster than the book's neat progression had suggested. If he pulled it now, the sauce would be mild, pale, safe. If he waited, it would go deeper, bitter at the edges, the way the good restaurants did it. His mother liked things burnt a little. His father liked everything underdone.

"Take it off," Hilary said.

"Leave it," Cullen said at the same moment.

"You're a pragmatist," Jeremy told him. "You'd eat it either way."

"I would," Cullen agreed, with dignity.

Mr. Rossi came around the corner with his clipboard, smelled the air, and said nothing. He had a policy of not intervening unless something was on fire, and he stood with his pen paused, watching, which Jeremy found more stressful than the sugar. The amber deepened. Somewhere past it there was a stage the book called dark, and past that, ruin. There was no thermometer clipped to the pan, no way to know if the sugar had passed 170 except by its color, which meant the whole decision came down to his eye and his nerve.

He thought of his father, who would say maybe he'd come, maybe not, keeping every option open until the moment passed. And his mother, who committed to everything and got hurt in exact proportion. Jeremy did not want to be either of them. He wanted a middle thing, a considered thing, but the sugar was not waiting for his philosophy. It was turning mahogany at the edges and the smell had shifted from candy to something almost like coffee.

He pulled the pan off the heat and poured in the cream in a fast, careful stream. The sauce hissed and boiled up and then settled, glossy and deep amber, darker than safe and lighter than burnt. He dipped a spoon and tasted it. Sweet first, then a grown-up bitterness underneath, and he stood there holding the spoon, honestly unsure whether it was good or whether he had ruined it and would know only when his parents tasted it, if his father came, if his mother got home before ten.

"It's good," Hilary said, reading his face.

"It's a gamble," Jeremy said.

At seven-fifteen his mother texted that she was stuck at work, could he box everything, they'd eat tomorrow. His father's text arrived a minute later saying he was five minutes away, he'd definitely be there tonight. Jeremy looked at the sauce, the chicken, the whole committed meal, and at the doorway, where Cullen was already unpacking a fork he had apparently brought from home.

"So," Cullen said, pulling up a stool. "About that gamble."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
The application was due by five o'clock, and Michael had forty minutes, a pen with a dying spring, and a question on the back page he could not answer. It asked whether he understood the terms of his employment. He stood between a rack of copper fittings and a display of paint samplers at Horner's Hardware, holding the clipboard the way his cousin Delphine held her phone, like evidence in an argument she intended to win.

The argument had started two nights ago at dinner. Delphine lived in Missoula, and her brother Vic lived in Columbus, and they had been fighting since they were children about everything from cereal to politics. This time it was Vic's boss, who had fired a coworker on a Monday for, as far as anyone could tell, waking up in a bad mood. Vic said that was life, that a boss could fire you for anything, that Ohio was an at-will state and so was everywhere else, basically. Delphine had laughed at him across the mashed potatoes. Not everywhere, she said. Not mine.

"Montana," she had said, tapping the table. "Look it up." Michael had not looked it up, because Vic had immediately launched into a story about a forklift, and by the time the plates were cleared the argument had been swallowed by the bigger family noise. But now, in the aisle of the hardware store, the question on the form looked suspiciously like the question his cousins had been fighting over, and the clock above the register said 4:21.

He found Emanuel first, crouched by the key machine, cutting a copy of a brass house key for a woman who kept describing her front door in unnecessary detail. Emanuel already worked here, three afternoons a week, and had been the one to tell Michael the job was open. When the woman finally left with her new key, Emanuel straightened up and cracked his back.

"Did you finish the form?" Emanuel asked. "McKenzie does the hiring at four-thirty sharp. She's strict about it. She once made a kid come back the next day because he was six minutes late."

"I'm stuck on the last question," Michael said. "It asks if I understand the terms. What are the terms?" Emanuel shrugged and said something about showing up on time and not stealing, which struck Michael as the terms of being a decent person anywhere rather than the terms of this job specifically. It didn't seem like the same thing, and the distinction seemed to matter, though he couldn't yet contextualize why. He carried the clipboard toward the paint counter, where Emerson was mixing a gallon of eggshell white, the machine shuddering through its interminable cycle.

"McKenzie hired you last summer," Michael said. Emerson nodded, watching the can spin. "So she can just let you go. Anytime. For no reason." Emerson said yeah, probably, that was how jobs worked, and Michael heard Vic's voice coming out of his mouth, Ohio in every syllable. "Except," Michael said slowly, and there it was, the thing he had half remembered from the dinner table. "Delphine's in Montana. She says there's a law. After you've been there a while, some probation period, the boss actually needs a real reason. A good cause. It's called the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, 1987. She kept saying it like a spell." Emerson tilted the can, checked the color, and said that Montana was weird about a lot of things.

At 4:28 Michael was in front of Ms. McKenzie's tiny office behind the registers, the form filled out except for one blank. She was older, glasses on a chain, and she took the clipboard and read it in complete silence while he stood there feeling the whole milieu of the store, the smell of cut pine and machine oil, settle around them like weather.

"Terms," she said at last. "You put 'not sure yet.'" She looked at him over the glasses. "That's a first."

"I didn't want to sign something saying I understood when I don't," Michael said. "My cousin in Ohio says a boss can fire you for nothing. My cousin in Montana says that's not true there, that there's a law from 1987, the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, so after a probationary period they need good cause. They can't both be right. Or they can, and it just depends where you are. I don't know which one this is."

Ms. McKenzie set the pen down. "Honest answer. You start Saturday, eight in the morning. If you're late I'll be in a bad mood, and you'll find out what the terms are here soon enough." She slid a lanyard across the desk, a name badge already printed, and Michael picked it up and read his own name in small blue letters.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
The automatic doors admitted Aiden along with a gust of October air, and he stood a moment in the produce section holding his mother's list, which he had copied onto his phone in the parking lot because her handwriting had deteriorated past reading. Chicken, four breasts. Lemons. The rosemary he would have to gamble on. His mother was stuck downtown; her deposition had run long, the lawyers asking the same question nine ways, and she had texted him at three o'clock to say the dinner was his if he wanted it. He wanted it. He had been planning the meal since Sunday, and the plan had grown grandiose in the way plans do when they exist only in a notebook: pan-seared chicken with lemon and rosemary, roasted potatoes, something green he hadn't decided on yet.

In the meat aisle he picked up the package closest to the back, where the cold had been working longest, and pressed two fingers against the plastic. At the far end, Justice was loading energy drinks into a basket with the seriousness of a man provisioning for a siege. "You're still doing that dinner thing," Justice said, coming over. "Friday night and you're buying potatoes."

"Friday night is a construct," Aiden said, and Justice laughed without asking what he meant, which was the arrangement between them.

Mr. Santos-Reyes from two doors down was at the deli counter, and he nodded at Aiden's basket as they passed. "Your mother mentioned you'd taken over the kitchen. She bragged, actually." Aiden said something modest and moved on, but the sentence stayed with him through checkout, through the walk home with the bags cutting into his palms, through the unpacking. He put his phone on the counter with a recipe open and set the oven to four hundred and twenty-five.

The problem surfaced at seven fifteen. The recipe said six minutes a side, but his stove ran either hotter or colder than whoever wrote the recipe's stove, and when he cut into the thickest breast to check, the juices ran pale pink at the bone. He stood there with the knife in his hand and the meal twenty minutes behind schedule, and Jessica, who had come over to work on their shared chemistry lab write-up and had instead been watching him cook from a stool by the fridge, said, "That looks wrong."

"It's not done. But if I put it back, the outside's going to be shoe leather by the time the middle's safe, and I don't actually know where the line is. People say look at the juices, people say cut it open, people say it's obvious. None of that is a line."

Jessica pulled out her phone and typed, and the cold air from the open freezer section seemed to follow her into the kitchen, bracing him the way it had in the store, sharpening the whole evening into something with edges. "Here," she said, and turned the screen toward him. US food safety agencies, an actual government page: chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.

Aiden stared at it. "We don't have a food thermometer."

"Mr. Santos-Reyes does. He's the kind of person who has a drawer full of them." She was already calling, and when he answered she put it on speaker, and the whole arrangement was made in under a minute: he would walk over, he had a thermometer in a drawer somewhere, no, it had never been used, it came with the grill.

While he was gone, Aiden set the half-cooked breasts on a plate and stood at the window watching the streetlights come on along their block. His father, who worked nights and ate at nine, would not care about pink juices; he would eat what was in front of him and say it was good. His mother would care. She had once thrown out an entire turkey mid-Christmas on the strength of a bad feeling about it, and half the family had thought her reckless and half had thought her wise, and nobody had had anything like a number. Aiden had spent two years of chemistry learning that his instinct about a result was worth nothing until it was measured, and he had spent seventeen years before that eating food judged by instinct alone, and both of those things were true, and he did not know yet which one he actually believed in.

Mr. Santos-Reyes arrived carrying the thermometer like a man delivering a verdict, a thin metal probe with a dial at the top. "My wife bought this in 2019 and we have never once used it," he said. "You're the first." He stayed, leaning against the doorframe with his coat still on, and Aiden slid the probe into the thickest breast at its thickest point, angled toward the center, and watched the needle climb. 138. 145. He returned the chicken to the pan, counted to nothing in particular, and stabbed it again. The dial settled at 168 degrees Fahrenheit, and Jessica, reading over his shoulder, said, "165 Fahrenheit, so that's past it, and 74 Celsius, so we're safe both ways," and Mr. Santos-Reyes said, "Well, there you go," and took his coat off after all.

The potatoes were overdone and the green thing turned out to be frozen peas, and his father came home at nine-fifteen and ate two breasts and said nothing about the third, which was still in the pan, probed and proven. His mother walked in at nine-forty with her heels in her hand, and Aiden handed her a plate. "How do you know it's done?" she asked, and he picked the thermometer up off the counter and held it out to her.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
The assignment on the board read "Self-Portrait in Graphite, due Thursday," and Owen had been avoiding it for two weeks, which was why he was now in the art room during lunch with a sheet of paper and a borrowed pencil he hadn't examined. He began with the eye, because everyone said never begin with the eye, and the darkness of it surprised him. It went down thick and oily, and when his hand dragged across the cheekbone a minute later, the whole shadow travelled with it, a grey smear over the face like weather.

Evan was at the next table constructing a cardboard armature for something he called a monument to procrastination, which he insisted was a serious conceptual piece despite the facetious name. He looked over at Owen's ruined cheek and winced. "That's brutal. What did you draw that with, a briquette?"

"The pencil by the sink." Owen turned it over. On the barrel, where a number should be, there was only a worn spot and a single letter, B, pressed into the yellow paint. He rubbed at his cheek with a kneaded eraser, lifting some of the grey, and the paper came up pilled and shiny where the mark had been.

Aaliyah arrived with her own sketchbook and a sandwich she didn't finish, and she spread her pencils out across the table in a neat row like surgical instruments. When Owen told her about the smear, she asked to see the pencil, held it to the window, and then pulled one of her own from the row. Hers was marked H. "Try this," she said. "Mine never smears like that."

He tried it. The line came out thin and pale, so light he had to go over the eyelid three times before it read at all, but when he swept the heel of his hand across it, nothing moved. The shadow stayed where he had put it, clean, faint, obedient. He sat back and looked at the two pencils lying side by side, the B fat with darkness, the H holding its thin silver mark.

"Why would they make them so different?" he said.

"Core's different stuff. It's graphite mixed with clay." Aaliyah said it the way she reported most facts, flatly, as if reading off an invisible card. "More clay and it's harder, makes a lighter mark, that's the H ones. Less clay, softer and darker, that's B." She demurred when he asked how she knew, shrugging one shoulder, saying only that her grandfather had been a draughtsman and had opinions, and that if Owen wanted real darkness he needed the B range and a fixative can, not a harder pencil.

Owen tested it. He took a 4B of hers and a 4H and made two squares side by side, then ran his thumb across both. The dark square smudged like wet charcoal; the light one barely acknowledged his skin. So it wasn't just a matter of skill or of holding his hand higher, which Ms. Villanueva had told him last week, arching her own hand over a demo like a surgeon's. It was the pencil itself, its inner composition, clay against graphite, and every pencil had been quietly declaring which it was all along, in a single letter on the barrel.

He worked through the lunch period on a decision. If he built the whole portrait in H pencils, nothing would smudge, and he could rest his hand anywhere he liked, and the face would be pale and precise and safe. If he used the Bs, he'd get the darkness he kept seeing in the mirror, the real shadow under the jaw, but every passage would be a negotiation with his own hand and the smear of it. He filled the cheek with layered H strokes, careful, controlled, and looked at it. It looked like a portrait of someone who had been through a paper shredder and reassembled. Polite. Bloodless.

Ms. Villanueva came in mid-afternoon to collect the drying rack and found him still there. She looked at his sheet for a long moment and said nothing, which he understood to be a verdict of some kind. He took out Aaliyah's 6B and went back into the jaw, pressing until the core whispered and the shadow bloomed dark and true, and he told himself the smudging was the cost of the dark, the way anything worth pressing for had a cost, though he couldn't have said whether that was wisdom or just a thing people said.

Aaliyah came back after her last class and found him with graphite on his fingers, his cheek, and somehow one ear. She laughed, then stopped, because he had gotten out a can of fixative and had sprayed the finished portrait in the corridor, and it hung there now, glossy, set, the dark jaw exactly as dark as he'd wanted. She studied it and then looked at the assignment sheet still taped to the door, and her face changed.

"Owen. Read the second paragraph."

He read it. Thursday's critique was a graphite transfer exercise; the whole class would lay their portraits face down on fresh sheets and rub the backs with spoons to pull mirrored prints, and the soft, dark, smudge-prone work would transfer rich and whole, while his hard H underlayers, the careful pale hours of them, would give up almost nothing.

Aaliyah had already laid her smudged sheet against the window glass. "Mine's going to print like a dream," she said, and taped it up beside his, face out, waiting for Thursday.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers.
story:
Madison had cleared the kitchen table of everything except the laptop, a stack of printed paper, and the bowl of popcorn that Nova was already demolishing. The coding club's timeline of algorithms was due Friday, and the three of them, Madison, Nova, and Maina, had been arguing about it since four o'clock.

"Binary search has to be the oldest thing on here," Nova said, tapping the printout with a buttery finger. "It's just guessing. People guessed before they computed."

"That's not evidence," Maina said. "That's vibes."

"Vibes are a methodology."

Madison had stopped listening in any serious way, because her program kept failing. It was supposed to play the number-guessing game she'd promised the club: the computer thinks of a number between one and a hundred, the player guesses, and the program says higher or lower. That part worked. What didn't work was her demonstration that the smart way to guess, splitting the remaining range in half every time, found the answer in at most seven guesses, while checking one, two, three, four in order could take a hundred. Her linear search loop ran fine. Her binary search returned the number 37 no matter what she fed it. She had been staring at the same twelve lines of code for twenty minutes, and her thoughts had begun to coagulate around a suspicion that the bug was somewhere she'd already looked twice.

She read the loop aloud, slowly, the way Ms. Weiss had told her to do back in tenth grade when she was failing chemistry. "Low equals one. High equals a hundred. While low is less than or equal to high, mid equals low plus high, divided by two." She stopped. "Wait."

"What," said Nova, whose mouth was full.

"Integer division. When low and high get close, mid stops moving, and the loop just hands back 37 forever." She changed one line, adding one before dividing, and ran it. Seven guesses. Then she typed a target of 99 and watched the program walk straight to it, halving the world each time like a butcher who never wastes a cut. She felt something in her chest unclench, and only then noticed that Maina and Nova had gone quiet and were watching her instead of the screen.

The argument, she realized, had not died while she debugged. It had migrated.

Maina could see that Madison had arrived somewhere and that Nova was about to claim victory, so she moved the popcorn bowl out of arm's reach, a diplomatic gesture that fooled no one. "Okay," she said. "So the poster needs a first date for binary search. We can't write 'vibes' on a poster that's going in the hallway." She pulled the club's reference book toward her, the fat one with the cracked spine that lived in Ms. Weiss's classroom, which Ms. Weiss had lent them for the week, saying only, "Bring it back drier than you found it," a condition nobody wanted explained.

Maina turned to the index while Nova narrated tangential trivia about the Moore School, which she claimed her uncle had attended, though her uncle had also once claimed to have invented the frisbee. Maina's finger went down the B's. Binary search. And there it was, in the entry's second sentence, plain as a receipt.

She read it out loud. "The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers."

Nova sat back. "My uncle," she began, and then gave it up. "Fine. Not the frisbee guy. The other uncle."

"Mauchly," Madison said, writing the name on the printout in blue pen. "Nineteen forty-six. The Moore School Lectures." She said it again as she lettered the card for the timeline, because part of her still didn't believe a person could put a date on an idea that felt older than dates, older than computers, older probably than the steppe her grandmother always said their people had crossed with nothing but horses and opinions. But that was the difference, she supposed, between an idea being in the air and an idea being written down where you could point at it. What stayed uncertain, and she said so, was whether the poster's question was really "when was it thought" or only "when was it caught," and the three of them looked at the timeline and did not resolve it.

The doorbell rang. Ms. Weiss stood on the step in her gardening gloves, holding a ceramic dish with one piece of lasagna in it, which she offered in exchange for the book being returned tomorrow instead of Friday. Madison took the dish. Ms. Weiss leaned past her, read the timeline upside down from the doorway, and pointed at the 1946 card with a gloved finger.

"Huh," said Ms. Weiss. "I would have guessed older."

"Everyone does," said Nova.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the second line of the staff, marking that line as the G above middle C.
story:
Olivier had claimed the garage as his own in October, when the car moved to the driveway for good, and now it smelled of cold concrete and the lemon polish he used on his mother's old keyboard. He sat on a milk crate with the keyboard across his knees, a pencil behind his ear, and a sheet of staff paper on the workbench beside a coffee can of screws. Sixteen bars. That was the assignment Ms. Sandhu had given them on Friday, due in two weeks: a melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, something that sounded like a person had meant it.

He could play. That had never been the problem. He could hear a tune in his head the way other people heard a conversation, whole and continuous. But between his ear and the page something kept going wrong, and today he had found out what. He had copied a melody from his notebook onto fresh staff paper, played it back from the page, and the whole thing had landed a third too low, warped and mournful, like it was underwater. He stared at the notes. The notes were right. He had checked each one twice.

Rylen appeared in the doorway holding two cans of soda, snow dusting his shoulders. "You said you'd be out here all day, so. Rations." He set a can on the workbench and leaned over the paper. "Why do you look like someone died?"

"Listen." Olivier played what he had written, then played what he had meant, the same phrase lifted back up where it belonged. "Same notes. Different piece."

Rylen squinted at the page. His finger hovered over the curl at the start of each staff. "This thing's sitting lower on yours than in the book." He flipped open Ms. Sandhu's handout, which Olivier had left on the bench, and put his finger there too. In the printed version, the spiral of the clef wrapped around the second line of the staff; on Olivier's page, it hung lower, circling the first line instead.

Olivier set down the pencil. Something opened in his chest, the way it did in math class when a stuck problem suddenly showed its hinge. He had learned the name ages ago, in some half-remembered lesson: "It's called the G clef," he said slowly. "Because the curl circles the second line. That line is the G above middle C." He hadn't really believed the name meant anything physical before. It had seemed like a decoration, one of those bits of ceremony adults insisted on. He had drawn it where it looked nice, and every note on his page had shifted to fit the new geography, all his careful pitches dragged down with the border.

"So the squiggle is doing the actual work," Rylen said. "The squiggle is the boss of everything after it."

"That's so strange." Olivier drew a new staff, and this time he watched his own hand, the pencil curling deliberately around the second line, feeling a little foolish and a little delighted, like being told a coin had a secret second face. "It's not naming the notes. It's placing them." He thought of Ms. Sandhu saying that notation was a map, not a picture, and he had assumed that was an affectation, teacher-talk for the poetry of it. Apparently she had meant it literally. A map with a moving origin.

They worked until the light through the garage door went from white to amber. Olivier redrew his sixteen bars, the melody climbing out of the mud, and then, in the eighth bar, he stopped. He had been avoiding a chord change all afternoon because he couldn't decide whether the tune wanted a bridge or a rest, whether to push into something new or let it circle back. Rylen liked the push. Olivier's mother, overhearing from the kitchen earlier, had hummed the version that circled back. He sat with his hands on the keys, playing both endings one after the other, and found that he honestly could not tell which one was truer, only that they were two different kinds of honest.

"Play the first one again," Rylen said. Olivier did. Then the second. The second one left a small door open at the end, unresolved, and he noticed that he kept leaning toward it, wanting to hear what came after the page stopped.

He wrote both endings, one above the other in the margin, and labeled them with a question mark, thinking he would ask Ms. Sandhu whether an unfinished cadence counted as finished. Probably she would say that was up to him. The pencil curl of the clef sat at the head of every staff now, exact and small, and he traced it once with his fingertip before closing the lid of the keyboard.

"So which is it?" Rylen asked, pulling on his coat.

"I don't know yet," Olivier said, and turned off the workbench light.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The hardware store shared a parking lot with Glendale Foods, and somewhere along the way the two businesses had stopped pretending to be separate, so a person could buy a hinge and a pound of smoked turkey without going outside. Laura had been hired for the hardware side, which suited her fine. Her interview with Ms. Lau had lasted eleven minutes and involved one question, about whether she could tell a flathead screwdriver from anything else in the drawer, and she could, so she started Saturday.

She had spent Friday night doing something she was slightly embarrassed to admit, even to herself: reading the federal child labor rules. It had begun as nerves, a way of feeling prepared the way other people laid out clothes. But the rules turned out to be unexpectedly gripping, in the way that any list of specific prohibitions is gripping, and by ten o'clock she had learned that under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant. Even in a grocery store deli. The specificity of it delighted her. Someone, somewhere, had imagined exactly this building.

Saturday morning, Melyna and Axel biked past the lot on their way to the creek and spotted her through the window, and Axel pressed his face to the glass until Ms. Lau rapped a knuckle on it from inside. He saluted. Melyna mouthed something that was either "good luck" or "you owe me five dollars," and then they were gone, and Laura turned back to the register, where her scanning thumb was already threatening to atrophy from disuse, since the hardware side had exactly four customers before noon.

At noon Ms. Lau came around the corner wiping her hands on her apron. "Renata called in," she said, naming the deli woman with the tone of a woman naming a recurring weather event. "I need you to cover the slicer for the lunch rush. It's easy. Thumb the guard, drop the ham, crank the dial." She was already walking toward the deli case, expecting Laura to follow.

Laura followed for three steps and then stopped, which felt, in her body, like an act of enormous foolishness. It was her first day. She was seventeen and newly in possession of a paycheck that was supposed to carry her through a summer of gas money and vinyl records, and without it she would be, as Axel liked to announce dramatically whenever he lost a five-dollar bet, destitute. She thought of the rules she'd read, and she thought of Ms. Lau's calm, practical face, and she found that the two could sit together in her mind without either one winning, which was not the feeling she'd expected.

"I can't," Laura said. "Under federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers. Even in a grocery store deli or a restaurant."

Ms. Lau turned around slowly. For a moment Laura braced for the apron to come off her own shoulders, metaphorically, though also possibly literally. Then Ms. Lau put two fingers in her mouth and whistled toward the back, and Axel came out from behind the pallet of mulch, where he had been crouching for forty minutes, holding a clipboard with nothing on it and wearing a name tag that said RENATA.

"He's my nephew," Ms. Lau said. "He does this for every new hire. If you'd cranked that dial, I'd have known you'd say yes to anything, and I can't use a person like that near the table saws." She looked at Laura with what might have been approval or might have been simply the end of a long-held bet with herself. "Also, you should know, that slicer hasn't worked since March. You'd have stood there cranking a dead machine while Axel took notes."

"So I passed by refusing to do something illegal that was also impossible," Laura said.

"Best kind of passing," said Axel, peeling off the name tag. Then he frowned at the deli case. "Although now nobody's made the ham, and I'm actually hungry."

Ms. Lau tossed Laura a sandwich from the case, then a second one toward Axel, who dropped his clipboard to catch it. "You," she said, pointing at Laura, "are on registers and the key machine. That I'll teach you myself, because the key machine can take a thumb, and the rules are much quieter about thumbs." She snapped her apron and headed back toward the deli, where she cranked the dead slicer once, out of what looked like habit, and the blade turned out to have been fixed on Tuesday.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide level measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record.
story:
Sophie had agreed to bring the tent, and Keven had agreed to bring everything else, so it was almost fair. The two of them set up at the far end of the clearing where Ms. Pham had said the ground drained better, working mostly in silence until the poles were crossed and the rain fly hung crooked and ascetic, a little grey roof over two sleeping bags and not much else. Veronika was still by the fire pit, arguing with a flint. Sophie's grandmother, who had invited herself on the trip the moment she heard about it, sat in a folding chair with a paperback she was not reading.

The problem was Ms. Pham's assignment, which was due the Monday after break. Sophie had to explain, to a real audience, how greenhouse gases trap heat, and she had to be able to read the carbon dioxide graph, the one that climbed in a jagged sawtooth across a whole century. She understood the pieces. Certain gases let sunlight through and slow the escape of heat; the graph showed the concentration rising. But when she tried to hold both ideas at once, the invisible mechanism and the patient line on the page, they slid apart, and she was left with two facts that didn't seem to know each other.

"I still don't get why you're doing homework," Keven said, unrolling a foam mat. "You could just denigrate the whole thing. Say the numbers are made up. Half the internet does."

"Then I'd have to know why the numbers are real," Sophie said. "Otherwise it's just picking a side." She took the printed graph out of the front pocket of her pack, where it had ridden folded into quarters, and flattened it on the picnic table with two smooth stones from the fire pit.

Grandmother came over, abandoning the paperback, and set her glasses on her nose. "What's this supposed to be?"

"Carbon dioxide," Sophie said. "Measured at a place called Mauna Loa. Every day, going back decades." She traced the sawtooth with her finger, the little rise and fall that repeated every year like breath. "The wiggles are seasons. The trend is the part that matters."

Veronika arrived holding a field guide she'd found in Ms. Pham's crate of supplies, opened to a branching diagram of birds. "This phylogeny is amazing," she said. "All the warblers on one tree." She set it down beside the graph, and Sophie looked at the two pages: one diagram showing what had descended from what over millions of years, the other showing what had accumulated over one century. Different clocks entirely, she thought, and yet both were just patient counting.

Keven leaned in anyway. "So where's the scary part? What's the number where it all goes wrong?"

"There isn't a switch," Sophie said slowly, watching the line climb. "It's more like a dimmer." She found where the line crossed the horizontal rule marked 400. Her eyes went along it to the year. "Here. The daily average passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the whole record." She checked the axis again. "May 9, 2013."

"2013," Grandmother repeated. She sat down on the bench without being asked to. "I remember 2013. I was teaching third grade that year. Nobody came to tell us anything." She touched the corner of the paper as if it might smudge. "You're sure about the date?"

Sophie checked it twice more, because the number had suddenly become personal in a way she hadn't expected. "Daily average. At Mauna Loa. It's the first time in the record." She heard herself saying it as if reciting, and stopped, and said it again in her own words. "The day the line crossed that mark, it was just a Tuesday to everyone I know."

"That's the part I don't buy," Keven said, but without his usual edge. "A line on a graph doesn't feel like anything."

Sophie considered that. He wasn't wrong; the graph was bloodless, and she had been trying to force feeling into it all week. But sitting here with the tent sagging slightly and the fire pit unlit and her grandmother's hand still resting on the paper, she thought the problem might run the other direction. The mechanism and the graph and the ordinary Tuesday in 2013 were all describing the same thing at different distances, like the phylogeny and the bird in the bush. You couldn't collapse them into one feeling. You had to hold them side by side and be honest that they didn't fuse.

"I don't need you to buy it," she said. "I need you to read it. Look where the line is when it crosses 400. Tell me what year you see."

Keven put his finger under the curve and followed it, lips moving slightly, and Veronika leaned over his shoulder. "May 2013," he said at last, and looked up. "So it's higher now."

"Higher now," Sophie said.

Grandmother stood and brushed off her jeans. "Then we'd better get that fire going," she said, "before it's too dark to see what we're doing." She picked up the flint from the picnic table and walked toward the fire pit.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
story:
The science museum had given each of them a laminated card at the entrance, a scavenger hunt that ended at a darkened hall on the second floor where a model of a DNA molecule, taller than a doorway, twisted slowly in the light. Alexandra stood in front of it with her card in her back pocket, because the real assignment was not the card. Mr. Tse had told them, on the bus, that whoever could explain the wall display to a stranger, accurately and without notes, would earn the last presentation slot in the seminar, and Alexandra wanted that slot the way she wanted very few things: quietly and completely.

Kyra got there first, which was how the argument started. "When it copies," she said, tapping the glass, "the new molecule is all new. The old one is a template. Like tracing." Waylon, who had been morose since the planetarium show he'd wanted to see had been booked out, shook his head. "No, it's all old," he said. "That's the whole point of copying. You keep the original." They looked at each other with the specific stubbornness of people who have both just enough confidence to argue and just enough doubt to keep arguing. "Alexandra," Kyra said, "settle it."

Alexandra had been about to say she didn't know, and something in her resisted that, not because of the slot but because she genuinely didn't know, and that bothered her more than losing would. Her mother, who mailed her things, had slipped a letter into her bag that morning, and Alexandra had read it on the bus. "Your grandmother taught me to knit by handing me the needle halfway through the row," the letter said, "so that half the stitch on the needle was hers and half was mine, and we finished it together. I think about that whenever I teach anyone anything." The image had stayed with her, half of something carried forward, half newly made, and now, standing in front of the twisting model, she found herself looking at the two strands of the helix as if they were two people holding a row of knitting between them.

"Wait," she said. She crouched to read the panel at the base of the display, which most people walked past because it was low and the model was tall. The panel showed a double helix splitting, one strand going left and one going right, each strand pairing with a new partner strand. She read it twice. "It's both of you, sort of," she said slowly. "Each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand. One old strand, one new strand, in each of the two copies." Kyra leaned down beside her, and Waylon crouched too, grudges suspended. "So my tracing metaphor isn't wrong," Kyra said, "it's just that the tracing keeps half of the original in the copy." Waylon frowned. "And I'm not wrong either, it's just only half of it survives intact." Alexandra said the word on the panel aloud, feeling it in her mouth. "Semiconservative. That's what it's called."

They moved on to the next hall, where the display was about what happened after the copying: the model unzipped again, a shorter molecule read off one strand, and that shorter message traveled out to a structure where it was read three letters at a time and turned into a chain of amino acids. Mr. Tse's assignment covered this too, transcription and translation, and Alexandra stood there trying to build the whole chain in her head, copying, then reading, then building. Kyra wanted to move on to the gift shop; Waylon had begun to cheer up, or at least to stop radiating gloom, and was copying the three-letter codes into his phone. Alexandra was slower. She had always trusted a certain kind of rationalism, the belief that if she understood each step she would understand the whole, and the panel gave her the steps, and still there was a moment where the steps did not yet add up in her mind, a gap between reading the words and being able to say them to a stranger without notes.

She tried it out on Kyra, who agreed to play the stranger. "The DNA splits, one strand gets copied letter for letter into a message, the message goes out, and out there it gets read in threes and each three picks an amino acid, and the amino acids join up, and that chain is a protein." Kyra said it sounded right, but Kyra would say that. Waylon, without looking up from his phone, said, "You said letter for letter, but is it actually the same letters?" and Alexandra opened her mouth and then closed it, because she did not know, and the panel was six feet away and she was too honest to pretend she'd read it carefully. "I'll go check," she said. She went back and read it and found that the message wasn't the same letters, and came back and corrected herself, and Waylon nodded once, which from him was applause.

She found Mr. Tse near the exit, by the Foucault pendulum, and asked whether honesty about the parts she hadn't verified yet would count against her. "Not at all," he said. "Say what you know, and say where you're guessing. That's the whole discipline." Alexandra thought of her mother's letter again, half a stitch carried forward, half newly made, and understood that what she was learning today would subsume both of her friends' half-right answers, and that her own answer would be half verified and half taken on trust, and that tomorrow she'd go back and check the rest. Then she walked to the tall helix, where a woman with a stroller had stopped and was squinting at the panel, and Alexandra said, "Can I tell you what it's doing?"

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
The food bank ran out of the meeting room at the community centre in October, so it moved into the public library, and that was how Colton came to be stacking cans of chickpeas between the biography section and the microfiche cabinets on a Tuesday afternoon in November. He had signed up because his guidance counsellor had inculcated in him, gently but repeatedly since September, that colleges liked to see service, and because Amina had said she would be there too, and because he had never actually been inside a line like the one that was already forming at the front doors at four o'clock. He had expected a handful of people, mostly older, mostly unhurried. Instead the queue curved past the returns desk, along the periodicals, and out under the borrowed-books sign, and it was still growing.

"You said it would be quiet," he said to Amina, who was taping a paper arrow to the carpet.

"I said it would be meaningful." She knelt on the floor, pressing the tape flat with her thumb. "Those are different words."

The coordinator, a woman with a clipboard and a lanyard, put Colton on intake, which meant standing at a folding table near the atlas stand and checking people in, saying welcome, trying not to look at anyone longer than they wanted to be looked at. He was clumsy at it. A man in a courier jacket gave his name in a low voice and Colton asked him to repeat it, twice, and hated himself for the second time. An older woman with a wheeled cart smiled at him like he was somebody's grandson, which he was, somewhere, just not here, not yet.

Amina, meanwhile, was working the end of the line, handing out numbered cards and small talk in equal measure, and it was there, near the new releases shelf, that she overheard the volunteer from the Anglican church say the number to nobody in particular.
