He was a big man, retired maybe, and he kept looking down the line and shaking his head like a man doing arithmetic he didn't trust. Amina caught the middle of it and moved closer.

"Nearly 2.2 million visits," he was saying to the coordinator. "In one month. March of this year. Food Banks Canada counted it for their HungerCount. A record for a single month, and that's just Canada." He said it quietly, the way you say a thing you've checked twice because you can't quite believe it once. Amina stood there with her stack of cards and felt the number settle somewhere below her ribs. She had grown up with the phrase "the working poor," a term that was really a kind of metonymy, the word "working" standing in for a whole life of shifts and buses and calculations at the checkout, and she had thought she understood it. She understood it less now, watching the line move one card at a time.

The twist, when it came, came sideways. Near the front of the queue, holding a numbered card and a reusable bag with a library logo on it, stood Kaya from Colton's Grade 11 English class, the girl who had read her essay on King Lear out loud in October with such flat, devastating calm that Mr. Vu had stopped pacing and just listened. Kaya, whose locker was next to the water fountain, who had lent Colton a pencil in September and never asked for it back. She saw him at the intake table at the same moment he saw her, and neither of them arranged their face fast enough.

"Hey," she said.

"Hey," he said. "It's, uh, table four, when they call your number." His prolix instinct, the one that filled silence with clauses, abandoned him entirely.

She nodded and went to sit by the large-print westerns with her card in her lap, and Colton spent the next hour being extremely busy. He thought about Mr. Vu, who had once told the class that a fact was not an argument, that a number only became a story when you decided whose it was. He thought about his own reason for being here, the line on an application, and how it suddenly seemed both completely true and completely insufficient, two ways of thinking that refused to merge no matter how long he held them together. He was still a person doing a good thing; he was also a person doing it partly for credit; both of those were facts, and he did not know yet which one he would put in the essay, or whether he would put either.

At closing, Amina found him carrying the last flat of tomatoes to the supply closet. Outside the tall library windows the streetlights had come on, and the line was gone, and the chairs were stacked, and Kaya had left through the side door without looking back, which Colton noticed and then made himself stop noticing, or tried to.

"Two point two million," Amina said, leaning against the book return. "In March. One month."

He set the flat down on the cart. "For HungerCount," he said. "It's a record."

"Come on," she said. "My mom's picking us up out front."

Colton pulled his jacket from the chair and followed her toward the doors, past the biography section, where somebody had left a book face down on the shelf, still open, mid-story.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Rachel had promised the painting to Maeve by Sunday, and by Saturday afternoon the gray was still wrong. It was a portrait of her grandmother's kitchen, mostly done, the kettle and the window and the oilcloth on the table, and through the middle of it ran a band of gray wall that she could not make consistent. On the left of the canvas, where the wall met the blue of the window frame, it looked almost warm, like concrete in sunlight. On the right, beside the orange oilcloth, the same gray looked cold, almost greenish, and she had repainted that section three times with paint from the same jar.

She set the jar down on the drop cloth and went to find her mother, who was on the phone in the hallway and held up one finger. Rachel waited, then went back upstairs without asking. The deadline was real: Maeve wanted to photograph the piece that evening for a portfolio she was submitting to a summer program on Monday, and she had been clear that she would drive over at seven whether the painting was finished or not.

Quincy arrived at four with two iced coffees and no plans to leave. He wanted company while he practiced the speech he had to give on Tuesday, a five-minute elocution on local water rights that he had rewritten twice and still hated. He stood in the doorway of Rachel's room holding his note cards and said, "So tell me if this sounds like a person wrote it."

"In a minute," Rachel said. She was holding the canvas up to the window light, tilting it. The gray shifted again, warmer near the blue, cooler near the orange, and it did this every time, in every light, and she was starting to think the paint was not the problem.

Quincy read his opening paragraph to her anyway, sitting on the floor with his back against her bed. It was about how disputes over the aquifer had become endemic in their county, every town fighting the same fight with the same arguments, and Rachel said it sounded fine, and he said it didn't, he wanted it to sound less like a paper. Then he noticed she wasn't listening and looked at the canvas. "The wall's two different colors," he said.

"It's one color," Rachel said. "That's the thing. Watch." She laid the canvas flat and covered the blue window frame with a scrap of white paper, and the warm gray went neutral. She lifted the paper and it came back. She covered the orange oilcloth and the cool patch on the right went neutral too. Quincy leaned in with his coffee sweating onto his knee.

She got her phone and typed gray looks different next to blue and orange. The first result was a scan of an old page, dense type, a diagram of colored squares. She read the name aloud, Michel Eugène Chevreul, a chemist, and then the line under it. "It's called the law of simultaneous contrast," she said, and read on. Published in 1839. It described how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She looked at the canvas, at the blue and the orange sitting on either side of her band of gray, and understood that she had spent two days repainting something that was not in the paint at all.

"So the gray isn't wrong," Quincy said.

"The gray was never wrong," Rachel said. "It's doing what grays do. It shifts toward the complement of whatever's next to it, and I kept trying to paint the shift away." She could adjust it, she thought, could nudge each section slightly so the shifts cancelled out, or she could leave it and let the wall read as two moods of the same room, the way her grandmother's kitchen had actually felt. She did not decide right away. She washed her brushes, which had gone stiff, and worked the paint out of the ferrules one by one, trying to resuscitate the smallest one, and thought about her grandmother standing at that counter in the morning versus the evening.

At ten to seven Quincy read the whole speech through, standing, and it was better; the water part landed and the ending was still soft but he said he'd fix it Monday morning. Rachel listened this time and told him the truth about the ending. Then headlights came up the driveway, and Maeve knocked twice and came in with the camera already around her neck. Rachel turned the canvas toward her and did not say anything about the gray, and Maeve stood in front of it for a while and said, "The wall does this thing. Left side, right side. Did you plan that?"

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2011 analysis of the Dunedin Study found that children with lower self-control were more likely to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions as adults.
story:
The rec center's staff room smelled of chlorine and burnt coffee, and Brooke was early for her mentorship meeting, which was unusual, because she had swapped into a shift that wasn't hers. It was Cohen's Tuesday. He had texted at four, "family thing, can you take it," and she had taken it, the way she had taken his Thursday and his Saturday, and now she was sitting at the scarred table with her sneakers ticking against the chair leg, waiting for Ms. Mensah.

Ms. Mensah ran the junior leaders program and held her mentorship meetings wherever there was a free hour, and tonight that meant the staff room between the vending machine and the lost-and-found bin. She came in carrying a folder of printouts, set down a thermos, and looked at the schedule taped to the wall, where Cohen's initials had been crossed out and rewritten so many times the paper had gone soft.

"Third swap this month," she said. Not a question.

"He texts last minute. I say yes because otherwise the littles get sent home." The pool, through the door, gave off a sound like slow rain, kids from the after-school group doing their level-four strokes. Brooke pulled the towel from her shoulders and folded it, needing something to do with her hands. "I don't know if I'm helping him or helping him fail."

Ms. Mensah didn't answer that. She slid a printout across the table instead, the way she did, making Brooke do the work. It was a journal article, flagged with a pink sticky note, part of a stack Ms. Mensah was reading for a course she taught on Tuesdays. Brooke read the heading: a 2011 analysis of the Dunedin Study. She had never heard of it. The children in the study had been followed for decades, and the analysis had measured self-control in childhood and then looked at what the children became. She read the finding twice. Children with lower self-control were more likely, as adults, to have poorer health, less wealth, and criminal convictions. She read it a third time, mouthing the words, because it was one thing to hear an adult say habits matter, which was wallpaper, and another thing to see it printed with numbers behind it.

From the doorway, then, Cohen saw the two of them bent over the same page, and what he noticed first was the pool towel folded on the table, still damp, because it was his towel, from his shift, and second was the look on Brooke's face, which was not anger exactly but something more like arithmetic. He had come to apologize, or to explain about the family thing, which was half true, and standing there he understood that the explanation mattered less than the pattern it belonged to. He put his hands in his pockets. "I can take Saturday back," he said.

"You can take more than that," Brooke said. She turned the printout around on the table so he could see it, tapping the sentence about criminal convictions with one finger, not as a threat but as evidence. "It's not about one shift. It's that the shifts are the thing." She didn't fully believe this, that was the honest part; she knew a New Zealand cohort from decades ago couldn't tell her what Cohen's Tuesday meant, and she knew, too, that she covered for him partly because being indispensable felt like a virtue she could bank. She said so. "I like being the one who saves it. That's mine to own. But I'm not covering Thursday."

Ms. Mensah poured coffee and watched them over the rim of her thermos, saying nothing, because the whole method of her mentorship was the belief that an argument a kid builds herself will underpin whatever she does next, while advice slides off by Friday. On the wall behind her there was a faded poster from some long-ago science camp, a boreal forest under northern lights, dark trees and a green sky, and Brooke found herself looking at it while Cohen read, thinking that the trees in the poster had grown ring by ring and that nobody could see the rings from outside.

"The littles are getting out of the pool," Cohen said finally, and he went to get the towels from the shelf, and there were only eleven of them because Brooke had used one and left it folded on the table, damp, ordinary, hers. He counted them twice. Then he picked up the folded one too, carried it to the laundry bin, and dropped it in.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
story:
The cleanup had spilled into the food bank's loading bay by eleven, which was how Hannah ended up inside, elbow-deep in a bin of donated cans while Marie-Ange held a clipboard outside. The neighborhood volunteers had gathered everything from the park and the alley behind the pharmacy, and somebody's grocery drive had produced six boxes of sealed food that needed sorting before the truck came at three. Mr. Gill, who ran the place, had said only, "Sort fast, sort honest," and disappeared into the walk-in cooler.

Hannah worked the dates first because that was the rule she knew. Anything past its date went left, anything within it went right. The bin smelled of dust and label glue, and her fingers found the stamped numbers faster than her eyes did, so that a can would be halfway to the reject box before she had actually read it. She had been at it for twenty minutes when the pile on the left grew large enough to look wrong. Nine cans, fourteen, a bag of sealed rice, all of it weeks or, in two cases, only days past the stamped date.

"Marie-Ange," she called through the propped door. "How much of this stuff is past date?"

Marie-Ange leaned in, saw the left pile, and winced. "That's a lot of garbage. Mr. Gill's going to lambaste whoever did that grocery drive."

"He'd lambaste me for throwing it out, maybe." Hannah held up a can of tomatoes, its lid unblemished, its label bright. "It's a week over. A week. That's it."

"You saw the sheet he gave us. Past date goes."

Hannah looked at the photocopied sheet taped to the table, the one with the two arrows and the word SORTABLE at the top. It said nothing about dates at all. She said so, and Marie-Ange said that everyone knew what past date meant, and Hannah said that she actually didn't, not exactly, and that she was starting to think nobody here did. Caleigh came in from breaking down cardboard boxes just then, wiping her hands on her shorts, and asked what they were arguing about, and the three of them stood over the reject pile like it was a crime scene.

It was Caleigh, scrolling her phone with wet thumbs, who found it first, on the food bank's own website, buried under a heading about reducing waste. "It says a best before date marks when a food's quality may start to decline," she read, "not when it becomes unsafe. So sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat." She looked up. "It's a quality thing. Not a poison thing."

"Best before," Hannah said slowly, trying the words out. "Not, like, deadline."

"Not a deadline," Caleigh said.

Marie-Ange pointed out that this was exactly the kind of thing people got sued over, and that she was not going to be the one to decide, and that anyway the clock was the clock: the truck at three, the shelves to stock, and Mr. Gill had already come through twice asking why the sorting table still looked like the beach at low tide. Hannah could feel the argument pulling her two ways at once, the caution she'd been raised on pulling toward the left pile, the plain language of the website pulling the other way, and neither side felt like hers yet.

She went to the cooler to find Mr. Gill, and did not find him, but found instead the cooler itself, its shelves half empty, its door propped with a case of dented soup. On the wall beside it, in marker on butcher paper, someone had taped a running count of families served that week, and the number was higher than the number of boxes on the shelves. She stood there a moment, letting the cold air move against her face, and understood that she was not going to solve the question of waste by lunchtime, or maybe ever, only this one box, this one decision, in the next hour.

When Mr. Gill finally emerged, Hannah was waiting with a can in each hand, one from the left pile and one from the right. "These are both sealed," she said. "This one's a week past its best before. Quality, not safety, that's what the site says. I checked the stamps and the seals myself. I want to put the sealed ones back in the sortable pile, but I want you to say yes, because if I'm wrong, it shouldn't be a seventeen-year-old's word."

Mr. Gill took both cans, turned them over, pressed the lids with his thumbs. Outside, the truck's engine turned over somewhere down the block, early, growling at the corner.

"Show me the line you read," he said, and Hannah led him to Caleigh's phone, still glowing on the sorting table, while Marie-Ange held the screen steady against the glare.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: For an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers.
story:
The automatic blood pressure machine sat between the photo counter and the shelf of compression socks, humming faintly, its cuff folded over the armrest like something patient. Alicia had walked fast from school because her father's letter was in her bag, and she wanted numbers to hold against it before the wanting curdled into dread. She jammed her arm into the cuff and pressed start while her breath was still shallow from the cold.

The screen blinked to life and gave her 148 over 94. She read it twice. Somewhere in her health class notes, from the unit she'd half slept through, those numbers meant something she associated with her grandmother's stroke, with the genealogy of bad hearts her father traced at holiday dinners, pointing at relatives like a man reading a map of shipwrecks. She stood in the aisle with her hand pressed flat to her sternum, doing the thing she always did when she couldn't sort feeling from fact, which was to externalize it, text it outward, make it exist outside her body where it looked smaller.

"148/94 at the pharmacy machine," she sent Phoebe. "Am I dying or is it the machine?"

Phoebe's reply took a minute, long enough for Alicia to notice the fluorescents buzzing. "You walked there? My mom says those things read high if you don't sit down first. Also you're seventeen. Also breathe."

Before Alicia could answer, the cuff hissed again on its own, restarting, and she yanked her arm out. "It does that," said a voice behind her. Mr. Fortin, from three doors down, was holding a paper bag with a stapled receipt and watching her with mild concern, the way he watched everyone, as though people were faintly interesting weather. "It rechecks if you leave the arm in."

"It says my blood pressure is terrible." She heard her own voice climb. "My dad's on medication for his and he wrote me this letter about taking care of myself and now apparently it's me too, it's the whole family, it's, like, inherited doom."

Mr. Fortin set his bag down on the counter beside the machine. "May I?" He didn't touch anything; he just looked at the chair, then at her. "When I was told to track mine, the pharmacist had me sit first. Sit quietly, about five minutes, feet flat on the floor, and rest the arm here, supported at heart level. She said posture and activity change the numbers. Rushed numbers are not your numbers." He said it the way he said most things, as if recalling it from a drawer.

Alicia looked at the chair. It seemed too simple to matter, which was, she suspected, exactly why it might matter. She sat, planted both feet, and settled her arm in the cuff so it rested level with her heart, and then she had nothing to do for five minutes except be still. She took out the letter and read it again, the actual paper this time, her father's cramped hand telling her he'd started walking every evening and cut back on salt, that his readings had come down, that he wanted her to know it wasn't doom, it was maintenance, like flossing. The pharmacy smelled of cardboard and menthol. Somewhere behind the counter a register opened and closed. When the machine chimed softly to signal it was ready, she was almost reluctant to break the quiet.

132 over 85. She stared at it, then at Mr. Fortin, who raised his eyebrows and said nothing pithy at all, which for him was a form of applause. She photographed both readings, the rushed one and the rested one, because the difference was the lesson, the whole lesson, and she wanted proof of it for herself and for Phoebe and maybe for her father, who loved evidence.

She texted Phoebe the two photos side by side. "Same machine. Same me. Sat still five minutes, feet flat, arm supported at heart level, and it dropped sixteen points. Sixteen. I ran in here like a maniac and basically measured the running."

Phoebe answered with a row of exclamation marks and then a second message: "So what you're saying is our whole family history of panic is also a measurement error. Start walking with me after school and we'll be immortal by June."

Alicia laughed out loud, an unguarded bark that made a woman at the photo counter glance over, and she mouthed sorry and pocketed her phone. Mr. Fortin had picked up his bag and was halfway to the door. She caught up with him at the sunscreen display, holding the letter against her chest with both hands, the paper warm from her bag and from the five minutes she'd spent reading it in the chair.

"Walking helps, right?" she said. "That's real, that's not just the sitting thing?"

"Mine came down with it," he said, and pushed the door open into the late light. "Your father walks too, I've seen him. Evenings, around seven."

She stood in the doorway a moment, watching Mr. Fortin cross the parking lot, then she took out her phone and typed to her father, no draft, no deleting: "I used the machine at Mitchell's Pharmacy. I did it right. Tell you tonight."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than 30 percent of its income on housing.
story:
Xavier clocked out at nine and carried two folded leases to the break room, where the vending machine hummed over a table still sticky from somebody's spilled slushie. He spread the pages flat and weighted their corners with a salt shaker he'd pocketed from aisle six and a roll of quarters for the register. The first lease was for a studio above the dry cleaner on Meridian, five hundred and eighty a month, utilities separate. The second was a room in a shared house near campus, four hundred and fifty, but with a utilities split he couldn't predict, and a landlord who had hemmed on the phone whenever Xavier asked what the electric bill ran in January.

He had been at this for three nights. He was eighteen, done with high school in June, starting at the community college in the fall, and his mother had said only one thing about moving out, which was that she'd co-sign if he showed her the math. So he was doing the math, badly at first, then less badly. He wrote his hours at the store at the top of a napkin: twenty-six a week at eleven fifty, which came to roughly eleven hundred and ninety-six a month before taxes, less after. He'd never calculated take-home before, and the gap between the two numbers annoyed him like a door left open in winter.

Agatha came in at nine fifteen for her break, bought the same gourmand's handful she always bought, dark chocolate and those expensive smoked almonds, and dropped into the chair across from him. "You look like you're doing homework for a class you haven't taken yet." He turned the napkin so she could see. She was starting at the same college, living at home, and she read his columns of rent plus estimated water plus estimated electric with the slow attention she gave crossword clues she intended to get without help.

"Here's my problem," Xavier said. "The studio is fixed. I know the number. The house is cheaper on paper, but the utilities could swing it either way, and the guy won't give me last year's bills." He tapped the second lease. "So I asked the current tenant. She said electric hits a hundred and forty in winter, sixty in summer, and water's flat. So I can average it. Ninety a month, call it, plus my share of internet." He added the column twice and got the same total both times, which felt like a small victory: five hundred and eighty for the house, all in. The studio, with the dry cleaner's landlord quoting utilities at a flat ninety-five, came to six hundred and seventy-five.

Agatha frowned at the napkin. "Do you know what that is of what you make?" She did the division before he could, lips moving. "The studio's over half. The house is about half. That seems like a lot, but is there a number where it becomes officially a lot?" Xavier demurred, not because he was shy but because he genuinely didn't know, and he said so, which she seemed to respect more than a guess.

Haydn swept in at nine thirty smelling of the produce back room, sat down without being invited, and pulled out his phone because he could not sit anywhere without pulling out his phone. "What are we arguing about?" Agatha told him, and he typed while they watched, unhurried, then turned the screen around. "Okay. In the United States, HUD says you're cost-burdened if you spend more than thirty percent of your income on housing." He set the phone face-up on the table. "So there's your number."

Xavier sat with that for a second. Thirty percent of his take-home, which was maybe a thousand and fifty after taxes, was three hundred and fifteen. Both apartments were nearly double that. He said it out loud and heard how it sounded, like reading a diagnosis off a chart. He thought of the moribund little notebook in his backpack where he'd kept a budget for two weeks in junior year and then abandoned it; the notebook was dead but the problem, it turned out, had been alive the whole time, waiting for him at exactly this table.

"So both options fail the rule," Agatha said. "Then what's the point of the rule?" Xavier looked at the two leases, the studio with its fixed cruelty, the house with its swinging one. "It's not saying don't move," he said slowly. "It's telling me the truth about how much I'll have left. I can still choose. But I know now that either way, I'm choosing to be squeezed, and I should pick where the squeeze is smaller and figure out the rest." He wasn't sure the rest was figureable. Maybe a third shift. Maybe asking about summer hours before he signed anything. He folded both leases, put the napkin with the house's numbers inside the second one, and slid the salt shaker back toward his jacket pocket.

"I'd take the house," Agatha said, standing, gathering her almonds. "Fixed is only better when it's fixed low." Haydn shrugged and scrolled on. Xavier carried the leases up front with him, asked the closing manager whether they'd need anyone full-time over the summer, and while the manager thought about it, he set both pages on the counter side by side and squared their edges against the till.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The dispute began in the third quarter, when the receiver for the home team stretched for the ball at the back of the end zone and the line judge waved his arms incomplete, and half the bleachers behind Alexandra groaned as one animal. Her father stood up. "He had a foot in," he said, to nobody and everybody. "You could see the chalk." Alexandra's uncle agreed too loudly, the way he did, and a man two rows down in a windbreaker turned around and said the toe dragged, clearly, and for a moment the whole aluminum bench felt like it might come loose from its bolts.

Alexandra had come to the game for Milla, mostly, who played outside back and had spent the whole season riding the bench, and for the afternoon itself, which was warm for October and smelled of cut grass and someone's grill three lawns over. The community field had no scoreboard to speak of, just a tilted wooden thing with numbers a teenager hung by hand, and no screen, no camera, nothing the man in the windbreaker could point to. He kept pointing anyway, at the air, at the spot where the play had happened and stopped happening. "Show it again," he said, as if the air owed him footage.

Milla found Alexandra at the fence during the break between quarters, hair stuck to her forehead, water bottle in hand. "You saw it," she said. "Tell me you saw it. Was he in?" Alexandra said she thought his heel came down first, maybe on the line, maybe not, and Milla made a frustrated sound through her teeth. "If they'd scored we'd have the ball back with time left. I'd actually get on. I know I would." She looked at the field the way she looked at homework she'd already decided she couldn't do, and Alexandra recognized the look, because she'd worn it herself all through junior year before quitting piano without ever saying she was quitting.

Logan was sitting on the grass near the fence with his phone out, recording the game in lazy pieces, and it was Logan who said the thing that changed the argument. "They should do what they did in sixty-three," he said. "Army-Navy game. CBS showed the first instant replay ever, December 7, 1963. Some director figured it out, Tony Verna." The man in the windbreaker turned around again, slower this time, the way people do when someone says something they want to check. "December 7," he repeated. "That's Pearl Harbor day." "Same day," Logan said, shrugging. "That's what my grandpa told me. He was watching."

Alexandra had been half-listening, thinking about Milla on the bench, thinking about her own bench, the piano bench, the years of it. But the detail snagged her. She looked it up on her phone, because she didn't trust Logan's memory about anything, and there it was: the first instant replay on television, CBS, Army-Navy, December 7, 1963, a system devised by a director named Tony Verna. She held the phone out toward the windbreaker man without saying anything, and he squinted at it for a long time. "Huh," he said finally. "Sixty-three." He sat back down, and somehow the play didn't seem worth as much to him anymore, now that it had a history behind it, now that people had been demanding to see it again for sixty years.

Here is what the windbreaker man wanted, though Alexandra only understood it later: he wanted the call to be right, yes, but underneath that he wanted the game to be a thing that could be known, a thing with a true answer waiting somewhere in a machine. His daughter played on the other team. He had driven two hours. When the fourth quarter started he stood alone by the fence with his arms crossed, watching not the ball but the lines, the chalk edges, the small gray truths at the margins of everything.

The fourth quarter was torpid for long stretches, both teams running up the middle, the crowd settling into a drowsy grumble. Alexandra found herself less angry about the call than everyone around her, and she tried to work out why. It wasn't that she thought the referee had been right. It was that watching Logan's fact settle over the bleachers had shown her something: that wanting to see it again was itself a kind of subterfuge, a way of pretending the game could be made perfect, when what she actually loved about it was that it couldn't be. A recording wouldn't emancipate anyone. It would just move the argument from the bleachers to a slower, more technical room, where people with better eyes than hers would disagree in lower voices.

Milla went in with eight minutes left. She was on for exactly one possession, got beat once on a switch, and made one tackle, clean and hard, and Alexandra stood up and screamed her name, and the man in the windbreaker glanced over at her, almost smiling, because his own daughter was forty yards away and he knew what the screaming was for. The game ended one nothing, a draw, which satisfied nobody and left the disputed play hanging there like a question with no answer key.

Afterward, walking to the car with her father, who was still muttering about the chalk, Alexandra said that maybe the foot was in and maybe it wasn't, and that she'd decided she was fine not knowing. He looked at her like she'd confessed to something. "You used to want everything proven," he said, and she said, "I used to want a lot of things," and unlocked the passenger door for him.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer.
story:
Lily taped the printout of The Broken Column to the back of the garage and sat down on the overturned milk crate her father used for hauling tomatoes. The assignment was due Monday: a formal critique, color and composition and symbolism, five hundred words, no biography. Ms. Sadeghi had said the word "formal" three times on Thursday, each time more slowly, and Lily had written it in her planner and underlined it twice.

She had chosen the Kahlo because it was the one painting in the textbook she could not look at for long. In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer. That sentence was in Lily's notes, copied from the caption, and she had read it so many times it had started to feel like a spell. Now she had to look at the picture itself, in her own backyard, with nobody around to notice how long it took her.

Kiera came through the gate at four, carrying two iced teas and a bag of pretzels. "You said you'd fail if you didn't practice out loud."

"I said I'd write something incoherent," Lily said. "Sit. Ask me about composition."

Kiera sat on the grass, shook the printout's corner flat where the tape had buckled, and asked. Lily talked about the vertical split down the torso, the strap that held the body together like a damaged column, the desert plain behind it, the absence of anything soft except the white cloth. Kiera nodded along and ate pretzels and occasionally said "okay" in a way that meant she was listening.

At five Jayda arrived with her own essay finished, on a Picasso, and immediately began to expatiate on how much easier Lily's life would be if she had picked cubism instead. "Angles," Jayda said. "Angles don't cry at you."

"They're not crying at me."

"They're crying while looking at you, which is worse." Jayda leaned closer to the printout. "I keep wanting to apologize to her."

Lily had not been able to name that feeling, and hearing it from Jayda made it worse, or better; she wasn't sure. She turned back to her draft on the clipboard, the one she'd written Friday night, and read the first paragraph aloud. It was all symbolism: the nails as pain, the tears as grief, the column as the spine fractured in the bus accident, which Ms. Sadeghi had said nothing about in class but which the textbook mentioned in a sidebar. It read like a book report wearing a costume.

She remembered, then, the museum in the city, two years ago, before any of this. Her mother had stood in front of a Kahlo self-portrait for a long time, longer than she stood in front of anything, and when Lily had tugged her sleeve and asked what was taking so long, her mother had said, "She's not hiding," and moved on. Lily had been thirteen and had thought it was a strange thing to say about a painting. She thought about it now with the printout sunning itself against the garage wall, the painted eyes still aimed outward, through the nails, through the tears, at whoever stood where Lily was standing.

She tore the draft in half and dropped the pieces on the grass. Kiera picked them up and smoothed them out on her knee without comment.

"You're being dramatic," Jayda said.

"I'm being a reactionary," Lily said. "That's what my second paragraph says. It says formal analysis is cold and the painting is personal and the two can't be in the same essay. That's a person defending the old way against the new way. I read it again this morning and it's just an excuse not to do the work."

Kiera held up the torn draft. "So do the work. What's the color doing?"

Lily looked. The sky was flat and pale, the ground cracked and dry, and against all that beige the green of the strap and the red of the wounds carried the whole weight of the picture. Nothing soft lasted anywhere in it; the body was a ruin in a landscape where even the mist at the horizon looked evanescent, as if it would lift and leave before you finished looking. And through all of it the eyes came forward, meeting hers over the nails and the tears, refusing to look away first.

She wrote for twenty minutes while Kiera and Jayda argued about whether Jayda's Picasso essay was due Tuesday or Wednesday. When she stopped, she had a sentence she liked: the composition holds the body upright with straps and structure, and the eyes do the opposite of what the body does, and the critique had to hold both, because Lily did not know yet which one the painting was actually about, and she wrote that down too, the not-knowing, as the last line of her paragraph.

"I still want to apologize to her," Jayda said, looking at the printout.

"Don't," Lily said. "Look back."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
The video arrived at 9:47 on a Tuesday night, while Ava was sprawled on the living room carpet with her laptop balanced on a cushion. Ann had sent it to the group chat with a string of exclamation marks: a grainy clip of a factory chimney belching orange smoke over a row of houses, captioned BREAKING. Joanna replied within a minute, "this is three towns over, we have to share this." Ava's thumb hovered over the repost arrow. Three thousand people had already pushed it into her feed, and the number was climbing each time she refreshed.

Her mother was out at a shift she'd picked up during her sabbatical from the community college, which had turned out to mean more work, not less, so the living room was Ava's alone except for the lamp and the sound of the refrigerator cycling in the kitchen. She watched the clip a third time. Something about it bothered her the way a wrong note bothers you before you can name the interval. The houses had old aluminum siding, the kind nobody installed anymore. The cars parked along the curb were boxy. She couldn't have said why that mattered, only that it did.

She called Ann instead of texting. "Where did you get it?"

"Some account with a bird logo," Ann said. "It had like forty thousand followers, so."

"So that makes it true?"

"Joanna already shared it. Her aunt commented." There was a pause, and then Ann's voice dropped into the tone she used when she wanted something. "If it's real, we're the ones who found it. Everyone's going to know we broke it first."

Ava said nothing. In the glow of the screen she typed TinEye into the search bar, because Mr. Tremblay, their retired neighbor who fixed bikes in his garage and had opinions about everything, had once mentioned it offhandedly while she was helping him carry a toolbox. "TinEye," he'd said. "Reverse image search. Been around since 2008." She had filed it away the way she filed away most of what he said, and only now, scrolling back through memory, did it surface. She took a screenshot of a frame from the video and uploaded it.

The results loaded slowly, and she caught herself holding her breath. At the top of the page was a sorting option. She clicked it and chose oldest first, because if the image had really appeared today, the oldest result would still be today, and the whole thing would be settled in her favor. Ann kept talking in her ear, something about how the local paper would owe them an apology for ignoring the last story. "Are you even listening?"

"Wait," Ava said. "Wait, wait."

The oldest match was not from today. It was from years ago, a news site's archive, a story about a fire at a plant in a town none of them had ever heard of, in a different part of the country entirely. The same chimney, the same orange smoke, the same boxy cars parked at the same angle along the curb. She scrolled through the other results and watched the image surface again and again across the years, borrowed and re-borrowed, each time wearing a new caption like a coat.

"It's old," she said. "The video. It's real footage, but it's from years ago. Somewhere else entirely."

Silence on the line. Then Joanna's voice, tinny, meaning Ann had put her on speaker without saying so. "So it's fake?"

"It's not exactly fake." Ava pulled the laptop closer and tried to find the words. "The image is real. It's the now that's fake. Somebody took something that actually happened and used it to make people believe it's happening here, tonight." She heard how thin the distinction sounded and pushed on anyway. "If we share it, we're not lying about the picture. We're lying about the date."

"That's not the same as lying," Joanna said, but without force.

"It's kind of the same," Ann said quietly, and Ava understood that Ann had known, or half-known, from the beginning, the way you half-know a rumor is too good to be true and share it anyway because the wanting absolves you. She looked at the repost arrow still glowing at the edge of the screen, then at the group chat where the clip sat in its little thumbnail frame, patient, waiting to be sent again by the next thumb, and the next. Misinformation like this felt endemic lately, everywhere at once, like weather. She couldn't fix the weather. She could fix this one drop of rain.

She typed into the chat, pasted the archived news link under Ann's video, and added nothing but the link. Then she stayed sitting on the carpet with the phone warm against her ear, listening to Ann breathe, until Joanna finally said, "Should I delete my post?"

"That's up to you," Ava said, although she wasn't sure it was, entirely. She refreshed the video's page one more time. Six thousand shares now, and climbing.

"Okay," Joanna said. "Deleting it."
